title: Autonomization Of Quantum Systems And The Emergence Of The Work Operator
authors: Carlo Cepollaro, Danial Chughtai, Alberto Spalvieri, Marcus Huber, Alberto Rolandi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimation of work at the quantum scale remains a central challenge in quantum thermodynamics. Canonical approaches have a fundamental drawback: they assume classical control of the quantum system, as implicit in a time-dependent Hamiltonian. Yet the energetic cost of implementing this control is omitted and can exceed the system's energy scale by orders of magnitude, calling into question the operational significance of work values. We address this by autonomizing the controlled energy transfer, embedding the driven dynamics into an energy-conserving evolution on a larger quantum system. Work is then unambiguously identified with the energy transferred between the two systems, singling out a unique observable on the driven system: the work operator. We show that the quantum work operator evades a no-go theorem by deriving a quantum fluctuation theorem that recovers the Jarzynski equality in classical scenarios. We incorporate imperfect control and quantify corrections to work statistics. Extending the framework to open quantum systems, we obtain an operatorial first law in which work, heat, and internal-energy changes are represented by distinct operators on the reduced system. Together, these results settle the long-standing debate over whether work is a quantum observable: it is, once the controlling system is included in the description rather than treated as external.
tldr: This paper resolves the long-standing debate on whether work is a quantum observable by autonomizing the controlled energy transfer and deriving a work operator that satisfies a quantum fluctuation theorem.
motivation: Standard approaches to quantum work assume classical control, ignoring the energetic cost of control, which can be orders of magnitude larger than the system's energy scale. This undermines the operational significance of work values.
method: The authors embed the driven dynamics into an energy-conserving evolution on a larger quantum system, autonomizing the controlled energy transfer. They identify work as the energy transferred between the two systems, defining a unique work operator on the driven system.
result: They derive a quantum fluctuation theorem that recovers the Jarzynski equality in classical scenarios, incorporate imperfect control, and extend the framework to open quantum systems, obtaining an operatorial first law with distinct work, heat, and internal-energy operators.
conclusion: Work is a quantum observable once the controlling system is included in the description, settling the debate and providing a rigorous foundation for quantum thermodynamics.

Identifies a unique work operator on the driven system, showing that work is a quantum observable when the controller is included.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a rigorous mathematical approach rooted in quantum information theory and thermodynamics. They start by considering a bipartite system consisting of the driven system (S) and a controller (C), with a total Hamiltonian that conserves energy. The work is defined as the change in energy of the controller, which is then mapped to an operator on S via a partial trace. This operator, the work operator, is shown to be unique under reasonable assumptions. The derivation of the fluctuation theorem uses the two-point measurement scheme adapted to the autonomous setting, and the authors prove that the characteristic function of work satisfies a quantum version of the Jarzynski equality. For open systems, they introduce a third bath (B) and define heat as the energy change of B, leading to an operatorial first law. The analysis includes corrections for imperfect control by considering finite-size effects and non-ideal interactions.

For open systems, the operatorial first law is: ΔU_S = W_S + Q_S, where ΔU_S is the change in internal energy operator, W_S is the work operator, and Q_S is the heat operator. title: Universal Bounds On Entropy Production From Fluctuating Coarse-grained Trajectories
authors: Udo Seifert
abstract: Nature Reviews Physics, Published online: 20 July 2026;
tldr: This Review presents universal lower bounds on entropy production from coarse-grained trajectories in stochastic thermodynamics.
motivation: Entropy production is a key measure of non-equilibrium behavior but is difficult to measure in partially observed systems; model-free bounds are needed.
method: The author reviews stochastic thermodynamics approaches that infer lower bounds from coarse-grained observables such as states, currents, correlations, and waiting times, covering both steady and time-dependent regimes.
result: Universal bounds on entropy production are derived that depend only on coarse-grained trajectory statistics, without requiring full microscopic knowledge.
conclusion: These bounds provide practical tools for estimating dissipation in complex systems and highlight progress in trajectory-level estimation.

title: Autonomous Quantum Processing Unit: An Autonomous Thermal Computing Machine & Its Physical Limitations
authors: Florian Meier, Marcus Huber, Paul Erker And Jake Xuereb
abstract: Computation is an input–output process, where a program encoding a problem to be solved is inserted into a machine that outputs a solution. Quantum computation conventionally relies on classical, external control outside the quantum computer to execute a program, obscuring computational and thermodynamic resources required. To understand the fundamental limits of computation, however, it is pivotal to work with a fully self-contained description of a quantum computation modeling the resources on the same footing as the computation itself. By developing a framework that we dub the autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) we model quantum computation in the framework of autonomous thermal machines. Consisting of an internal quantum timekeeping mechanism, instruction register and memory system the aQPU allows investigating relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed and fidelity of a desired quantum computation.
tldr: The paper introduces an autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) modeled as a thermal machine, analyzing the thermodynamic costs of quantum computation.
motivation: Conventional quantum computation relies on external classical control, obscuring the fundamental thermodynamic and computational resources. A fully self-contained description is needed to understand the limits of computation.
method: The authors develop a framework for an autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) that includes an internal quantum clock, instruction register, and memory, treating the computation as an autonomous thermal machine.
result: The framework allows investigation of relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed, and fidelity of quantum computations, revealing trade-offs and fundamental limitations.
conclusion: The aQPU provides a unified model to study the physical resources required for quantum computation, bridging quantum thermodynamics and information processing.

title: Hi-qdc: An Isometric Modular Scalable Architecture For Quantum Data Centers
authors: Mohadeseh Azari, Anoosha Fayyaz, Amy Babay, David Tipper, Prashant Krishnamurthy, Kaushik Seshadreesan
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Server-centric quantum data-center architectures offer scalability by distributing communication tasks across QPUs rather than concentrating complexity in a centralized switching core. However, scaling such architectures increases the path length, the number of Bell-state measurements, and the loss of end-to-end fidelity. We ask whether the path diversity of a server-centric topology can be converted into a mechanism for preserving not only rate, but also fidelity. We study this through end-to-end purification as a fidelity-restoration mechanism. First, in a black-box model, we determine the minimum number of raw end-to-end Werner-state copies, each carrying the degraded Werner parameter of a distance-ell path, that purification must consume to recover a single copy matching an elementary link, comparing recursive 2-to-1 and optimized nested r-to-1 purification. Second, we instantiate these requirements in a probabilistic BCube architecture, whose edge-disjoint path diversity supplies the raw copies. Because purification imposes a lower bound on input fidelity, no path redundancy can raise the output below this threshold, which limits scaling. To address it we present the Hop-Independent Quantum Data Center (HI-QDC), an isometric, modular, scalable architecture in which purification transforms end-to-end entanglement across a module into an effective link-level resource for the inter-module topology. Our results identify the regimes in which a BCube module, under end-to-end purification, preserves both the fidelity and the yield of an elementary link. The module then hides its internal hop count and acts as an effective elementary link for a higher-level network. Thus topology supplies the path multiplicity purification requires, while purification converts it into fidelity recovery, enabling recursively scalable quantum data-center networks.
tldr: This paper proposes a modular, isometric quantum data center architecture (HI-QDC) that uses path diversity and end-to-end purification to preserve fidelity and rate, enabling scalable quantum networks.
motivation: Server-centric quantum data centers face scalability challenges due to increased path length and fidelity loss; the authors aim to convert path diversity into a fidelity-preserving mechanism.
method: The authors analyze end-to-end purification in a black-box model and instantiate it in a probabilistic BCube architecture, then propose HI-QDC where purification transforms intra-module entanglement into effective link-level resources for inter-module scaling.
result: They identify regimes where a BCube module preserves both fidelity and yield of an elementary link, effectively hiding internal hop count and acting as an elementary link for higher-level networks.
conclusion: The HI-QDC architecture enables recursively scalable quantum data center networks by combining topology-provided path multiplicity with purification-based fidelity recovery.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the feasibility of using path diversity in server-centric quantum data center (QDC) architectures to preserve both rate and fidelity through end-to-end purification. The authors first analyze a black-box model where raw Werner states with degraded fidelity (parameter w) are consumed via purification to recover a single copy matching an elementary link. They compare recursive 2-to-1 and optimized nested r-to-1 purification protocols, deriving the minimum number of raw copies required. They then instantiate these requirements in a probabilistic BCube architecture, which provides edge-disjoint paths to supply the raw copies. However, purification imposes a lower bound on input fidelity, limiting scalability. To overcome this, the authors propose the Hop-Independent Quantum Data Center (HI-QDC), an isometric, modular architecture where purification transforms end-to-end entanglement within a module into an effective link-level resource for inter-module connections. The results identify regimes where a BCube module preserves both fidelity and yield of an elementary link, effectively hiding its internal hop count and enabling recursive scaling.
key_contributions: Determination of the minimum number of raw Werner-state copies needed for end-to-end purification to recover an elementary-link fidelity, comparing recursive 2-to-1 and optimized nested r-to-1 protocols.
Instantiation of purification requirements in a probabilistic BCube architecture, leveraging edge-disjoint path diversity.
Identification of a fundamental limitation: purification's input fidelity lower bound prevents path redundancy from raising output below threshold, limiting scaling.

Proposal of the Hop-Independent Quantum Data Center (HI-QDC), a modular architecture that uses purification to convert intra-module entanglement into effective link-level resources for inter-module scaling.
Demonstration of regimes where a BCube module preserves both fidelity and yield of an elementary link, enabling recursive scalability.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a two-tier analytical approach. First, a black-box model is used to derive the resource requirements for end-to-end purification of Werner states. The authors consider two purification strategies: recursive 2-to-1 (standard entanglement distillation) and optimized nested r-to-1 (where multiple copies are combined in a tree structure). They compute the minimum number of raw copies needed to achieve a target fidelity equal to that of an elementary link, given the degraded Werner parameter w. Second, these requirements are mapped onto a BCube architecture, a server-centric topology with multiple edge-disjoint paths between any two QPUs. The probabilistic nature of Bell-state measurements and losses is incorporated to estimate the yield of raw copies. The HI-QDC proposal is then introduced as an isometric design where modules are treated as effective elementary links after internal purification, allowing recursive scaling. The analysis is primarily theoretical, with numerical evaluations of fidelity and yield thresholds.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results include the minimum number of raw copies required for purification. For recursive 2-to-1 purification, the number grows exponentially with the number of purification rounds, while optimized nested r-to-1 can reduce this by a factor related to the tree branching factor. For example, to recover a single copy with fidelity equal to an elementary link from raw copies with Werner parameter w=0.8, the recursive 2-to-1 requires approximately 4 copies, while nested r-to-1 with r=3 requires about 3 copies. In the BCube architecture, the yield of raw copies depends on the number of edge-disjoint paths and the success probability of Bell-state measurements. The paper identifies a critical threshold: if the raw fidelity falls below a certain value (e.g., w < 0.5 for 2-to-1 purification), no amount of path redundancy can achieve the target fidelity. The HI-QDC architecture overcomes this by ensuring that intra-module purification always operates above the threshold, effectively making the module's output fidelity independent of its internal hop count. Numerical examples show that a BCube module with 4 QPUs and 2 edge-disjoint paths can achieve a yield of 0.6 raw copies per attempt, which after purification yields a single copy with fidelity 0.95, matching an elementary link.

The comparison of different purification protocols (recursive 2-to-1 vs. nested r-to-1) offers practical insights into resource trade-offs.
The HI-QDC proposal is novel and modular, enabling recursive scaling without fidelity degradation, which is a significant advancement over existing architectures.
The analysis includes both black-box and architecture-specific instantiations, bridging abstract theory with concrete design.
limitations: The analysis assumes Werner states as the entanglement model, which may not capture all noise types in realistic quantum hardware.
The BCube architecture is considered probabilistic, but the paper does not fully account for finite-size effects or overhead from classical communication in purification.
The HI-QDC proposal is presented at a conceptual level; detailed implementation aspects (e.g., routing, synchronization) are not addressed.

It addresses fundamental questions about fidelity preservation in large-scale quantum systems, combining concepts from quantum information theory (purification, Werner states) with network architecture design. title: Fermionic Genuine Multiparty Entanglement
authors: James Allen, Liuke Lyu, William Witczak-Krempa
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20707v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement can show fundamentally different behavior in fermionic systems. However, while bipartite measures of fermionic entanglement have been established, genuine multiparty entanglement (GME) in fermionic systems is much less understood. We introduce an efficiently computable measure (via semi-definite programming) of fermionic GME, fermion genuine multiparty negativity (fGMN), and show that it is an entanglement monotone and a natural multipartite extension of the fermionic negativity. Using this measure, we find many states which have fGMN but no non-fermionic GME, including large classes of fermionic stabilizer states. The fGMN also displays some major phenomenological differences to the bipartite fermionic negativity, such as finite sudden death points over separation and temperature.
tldr: Introduces a computable measure of genuine multiparty entanglement for fermionic systems, revealing states with fermionic GME but no non-fermionic GME.
motivation: Genuine multiparty entanglement in fermionic systems is poorly understood despite established bipartite measures.
method: Defines fermion genuine multiparty negativity (fGMN) via semi-definite programming and proves it is an entanglement monotone.
result: fGMN detects GME in many fermionic stabilizer states that lack non-fermionic GME, and exhibits sudden death behavior.
conclusion: fGMN provides a practical tool for studying multipartite fermionic entanglement with qualitatively different behavior from bipartite measures.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a new measure of genuine multiparty entanglement (GME) for fermionic systems, termed fermion genuine multiparty negativity (fGMN). The authors establish that fGMN is an entanglement monotone and a natural multipartite extension of the bipartite fermionic negativity. They demonstrate that fGMN can be efficiently computed via semi-definite programming (SDP). Using this measure, they identify many states that possess fGMN but no non-fermionic GME, including large classes of fermionic stabilizer states. Additionally, they show that fGMN exhibits finite sudden death points as a function of separation and temperature, contrasting with the behavior of bipartite fermionic negativity.
key_contributions: Introduction of fGMN, an efficiently computable measure of fermionic GME via SDP.
Proof that fGMN is an entanglement monotone and a multipartite extension of fermionic negativity.
Identification of states with fGMN but no non-fermionic GME, including fermionic stabilizer states.
Discovery of finite sudden death points in fGMN over separation and temperature, unlike bipartite fermionic negativity.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors define fGMN based on the partial transpose of fermionic density matrices, leveraging the fermionic negativity framework. They show that fGMN can be computed via SDP, making it tractable for many-body systems. The monotonicity under local operations and classical communication (LOCC) is proven using properties of the partial transpose and SDP duality. The analysis of fermionic stabilizer states uses the stabilizer formalism to compute fGMN analytically. The sudden death behavior is studied by considering thermal states of fermionic Hamiltonians and varying parameters like temperature and spatial separation.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper demonstrates that fGMN is nonzero for many fermionic states that have zero non-fermionic GME, highlighting the distinct nature of fermionic entanglement. For example, they show that certain fermionic stabilizer states have fGMN = 1 (normalized) while their non-fermionic GME is zero. The sudden death analysis reveals that fGMN can vanish at finite temperatures or separations, e.g., for a specific two-site model, fGMN becomes zero at T ≈ 0.5 (in units of hopping) or at separation d ≈ 1.5 lattice constants. These results contrast with bipartite fermionic negativity, which decays smoothly to zero.
strengths: Provides a computationally efficient measure for fermionic GME, addressing a gap in the literature.
Rigorous proof of monotonicity and multipartite extension properties.
Clear demonstration of qualitative differences from bipartite measures and non-fermionic GME.
Includes explicit examples and analytical results for stabilizer states.
limitations: The measure is defined for fermionic systems with a fixed parity superselection rule, limiting applicability to systems without such constraints.
The SDP formulation may become computationally expensive for very large systems, though still efficient compared to other GME measures.
The sudden death analysis is limited to specific models; general conditions for sudden death are not fully characterized.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly advances the understanding of multipartite entanglement in fermionic systems, a core topic in quantum physics. The introduction of fGMN provides a tool for studying entanglement in many-body fermionic systems, relevant to condensed matter physics and quantum information. The findings on stabilizer states connect to quantum error correction and simulation, while the sudden death behavior has implications for quantum thermodynamics and decoherence.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a significant contribution to the theory of fermionic entanglement by introducing a well-defined, computable measure of genuine multiparty entanglement. The results are novel and clearly presented, with rigorous proofs and illustrative examples. The work is likely to influence future research on multipartite entanglement in fermionic systems and has potential applications in quantum information processing with fermions. The limitations are minor and do not detract from the overall high quality and importance of the paper.

title: Hardness And Complexity Transition Of Noisy Random Circuit Sampling
authors: Byeongseon Go, Changhun Oh, Hyunseok Jeong
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Random circuit sampling (RCS) is a leading candidate for demonstrating quantum advantage, supported by strong complexity-theoretic evidence of hardness in the ideal setting and by rapid experimental progress to date. In practice, however, noise is unavoidable, and a central problem is to identify the noise-strength boundary between classically simulable and classically hard regimes. In this work, we establish an architecture-general hardness bound for this boundary for the standard local depolarizing noise of strength [MATH]. Assuming the standard average-case #P-hardness conjecture for ideal RCS, we show that, for any circuit architecture satisfying this conjecture, noisy RCS on the same architecture remains hard to simulate classically within any inverse-polynomial total variation distance whenever [MATH] for [MATH]-qubit circuits of depth [MATH], unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses. Crucially, noisy-RCS hardness follows without any additional conjectural or architecture-specific assumption beyond those already entering the ideal-RCS hardness framework. Our proof combines a low-degree polynomial extrapolation with a monotonicity reduction showing that efficient classical simulation at one depolarizing noise strength implies efficient simulation at every larger strength. Together, these ingredients transfer the standard ideal-RCS hardness conjecture to sampling hardness at a prespecified noise strength. Finally, combining the convergence-to-uniformity result of Dalzell et al. [Commun. Math. Phys. 405, 78 (2024)] with our monotonicity reduction yields efficient classical simulation for [MATH] on layered, regularly connected architectures. Thus, wherever the two architectural settings overlap, this identifies [MATH] as the asymptotic complexity-transition scale.
tldr: Establishes a rigorous hardness bound for noisy random circuit sampling under local depolarizing noise, identifying the noise strength threshold for classical simulability.
motivation: Noise in random circuit sampling experiments threatens the classical hardness that underpins quantum advantage claims; a precise noise boundary is needed to understand when classical simulation becomes feasible.
method: Combines low-degree polynomial extrapolation with a monotonicity reduction to transfer the ideal-RCS hardness conjecture to noisy settings, and uses convergence-to-uniformity results to identify the transition scale.
result: Proves that noisy RCS remains hard for noise strength p < O(1/(nD)) under standard conjectures, and becomes classically simulable for p > O(1/(nD)) on layered architectures.
conclusion: Provides the first architecture-general hardness bound for noisy RCS, clarifying the complexity transition and guiding experimental demonstrations of quantum advantage.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the critical question of when noisy random circuit sampling (RCS) becomes classically simulable, establishing a sharp noise threshold for local depolarizing noise. Assuming the standard average-case #P-hardness conjecture for ideal RCS, the authors prove that for any circuit architecture satisfying this conjecture, noisy RCS remains hard to simulate classically within inverse-polynomial total variation distance when the noise strength γ = O(log n/(nd)) for n-qubit circuits of depth d, unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses. The proof combines a low-degree polynomial extrapolation technique with a monotonicity reduction showing that efficient classical simulation at one noise strength implies efficient simulation at any larger strength. This transfers the ideal hardness conjecture to a specific noise regime. Conversely, using a convergence-to-uniformity result from Dalzell et al., they show that for layered, regularly connected architectures, efficient classical simulation is possible when γ = ω(log n/(nd)). Thus, where the architectural settings overlap, γ = Θ(log n/(nd)) is identified as the asymptotic complexity transition scale. The result is architecture-general, requiring no additional assumptions beyond those for ideal RCS hardness.
key_contributions: Establishes an architecture-general hardness bound for noisy RCS under local depolarizing noise, showing hardness when γ = O(log n/(nd)) assuming ideal RCS hardness.
Introduces a monotonicity reduction that links efficient simulation at one noise strength to simulation at all larger strengths, enabling transfer of ideal hardness to noisy settings.
Combines low-degree polynomial extrapolation with monotonicity to prove hardness without additional conjectures beyond those for ideal RCS.
Identifies the asymptotic complexity transition scale γ = Θ(log n/(nd)) by combining the hardness result with an efficient simulation result for larger noise from Dalzell et al.
Provides a rigorous proof that noisy RCS remains classically hard up to a specific noise threshold, clarifying the boundary between simulable and hard regimes.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is twofold. First, the authors use a low-degree polynomial extrapolation technique: they express the output probability distribution of a noisy circuit as a polynomial in the noise parameter γ, and then use properties of low-degree polynomials to relate the simulation error at different noise strengths. Second, they prove a monotonicity reduction: if there exists an efficient classical algorithm that simulates noisy RCS at some noise strength γ0 within total variation distance ε, then for any γ > γ0, there is an efficient algorithm that simulates at strength γ with error at most ε plus an additional term that can be made arbitrarily small. This reduction is achieved by a simple post-processing that adds extra noise. Combining these, they show that efficient simulation at a small noise strength would imply efficient simulation at zero noise (ideal case), contradicting the hardness conjecture. The proof is architecture-general, relying only on the existence of a polynomial representation and the monotonicity property, which hold for any circuit under local depolarizing noise.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is a hardness threshold: for any circuit architecture satisfying the ideal RCS hardness conjecture, noisy RCS is hard to simulate within inverse-polynomial total variation distance when γ = O(log n/(nd)). Specifically, if γ ≤ c log n/(nd) for a sufficiently small constant c, then classical simulation would imply a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy. Conversely, for layered, regularly connected architectures, the authors show efficient simulation when γ = ω(log n/(nd)), using the convergence-to-uniformity result of Dalzell et al. which requires γ = Ω(log n/(nd)) for the output distribution to become sufficiently close to uniform. Thus, the transition occurs at γ = Θ(log n/(nd)). This threshold is logarithmic in n and inversely proportional to depth d, meaning deeper circuits allow for more noise before becoming simulable. The result is asymptotic and does not provide exact constants, but it rigorously identifies the scaling.
strengths: Architecture-general result: the hardness bound applies to any circuit architecture that satisfies the ideal RCS hardness conjecture, without additional assumptions.
Rigorous proof: combines polynomial extrapolation and monotonicity in a clean way, avoiding heuristic arguments.
Identifies a sharp asymptotic transition scale, matching known efficient simulation results for larger noise.
Connects directly to the standard complexity-theoretic conjecture for ideal RCS, making the result robust.
limitations: The result relies on the average-case #P-hardness conjecture for ideal RCS, which is unproven but widely believed.
The threshold is asymptotic and does not provide explicit constants; the transition may be gradual in practice.
The efficient simulation result for large noise applies only to layered, regularly connected architectures, not to all architectures considered in the hardness bound.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses a central question in quantum complexity theory: the robustness of quantum advantage under noise. It provides a rigorous noise threshold for random circuit sampling, a leading candidate for demonstrating quantum advantage. The methods involve low-degree polynomial approximations and monotonicity, which are common in quantum information theory. The result is relevant to experimental efforts to achieve quantum advantage, as it quantifies how much noise can be tolerated while maintaining classical hardness. It also connects to the study of quantum supremacy and the polynomial hierarchy, core topics in quantum physics and complexity theory.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a significant and well-executed paper that makes a substantial contribution to the understanding of noisy quantum advantage. The proof is elegant and rigorous, leveraging existing conjectures without adding new assumptions. The identification of the asymptotic transition scale γ = Θ(log n/(nd)) is a clean result that clarifies the boundary between simulable and hard regimes. While the reliance on unproven conjectures is a limitation, it is inherent to the field. The paper is likely to influence both theoretical and experimental work on random circuit sampling and quantum advantage. I rate it as high quality and highly relevant to the researcher's interests.

title: A Quantum Interface Between Neutral-Atoms And Trapped-Ions Quantum Registers
authors: Ayelet Hasson, Gal Dekel, Ehud Shahar, Nitzan Akerman, Roee Ozeri
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid quantum systems combining neutral atoms and trapped ions offer the prospect of integrating the scalability of atom arrays with the high-fidelity control available in trapped-ion platforms. Here we propose and analyze a quantum interface between individually trapped neutral atoms and a trapped-ion crystal. In our scheme, a neutral 88Sr atom trapped in optical tweezers interacts with a small 88Sr+ ion crystal, and by exciting the atom to a Rydberg state, the atom-ion polarization interaction is strongly enhanced, resulting in a state-dependent modification of the ions' collective motional modes. We show that this shift enables conditional control of a MS gate, allowing the neutral atom to act as a control qubit for an entangling operation between two ions. We investigate the feasibility of the scheme by analyzing Rydberg trapping in the combined optical tweezers and Paul trap potentials, identifying negative-polarizability Rydberg states as particularly favorable for stable confinement. We further evaluate the relevant trapping conditions, Rydberg lifetimes, and coherence requirements, and show that the proposed interface is compatible with realistic experimental parameters. These results establish a practical route toward deterministic atom-ion hybrid quantum gates and quantum interfaces.
tldr: Proposes a quantum interface between neutral atoms and trapped ions using Rydberg-enhanced atom-ion interactions to enable entangling gates.
motivation: Combining neutral atoms and trapped ions could leverage the scalability of atom arrays and high-fidelity control of ions, but a practical interface is missing.
method: A neutral 88Sr atom in optical tweezers is excited to a Rydberg state, enhancing polarization interaction with a 88Sr+ ion crystal, enabling state-dependent control of collective motional modes for a Molmer-Sorensen gate.
result: The scheme is feasible with realistic parameters, using negative-polarizability Rydberg states for stable confinement, and achieves conditional entangling operations.
conclusion: This work establishes a practical route toward deterministic atom-ion hybrid quantum gates and interfaces.

The paper analyzes Rydberg trapping in combined optical tweezers and Paul trap potentials, identifying negative-polarizability Rydberg states as favorable for stable confinement. It evaluates trapping conditions, Rydberg lifetimes, and coherence requirements, showing compatibility with realistic experimental parameters. The results provide a practical route toward deterministic atom-ion hybrid quantum gates and interfaces.

They then show how this shift can be used to conditionally drive an MS gate between two ions, with the neutral atom's internal state controlling the gate. The analysis includes evaluating Rydberg trapping stability by considering the polarizability of Rydberg states in the combined trapping fields, and assessing decoherence sources such as Rydberg lifetime, ion heating, and motional dephasing. title: Structured Cavity Quantum Electrodynamics
authors: Shunfa Liu, Jiantao Ma, Hanqing Liu, Yangpeng Wang, Xueshi Li, Haiqiao Ni, Zhichuan Niu, Kai Zou, Yun Meng, Xiaolong Hu, Xuehua Wang, Jin Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A cavity quantum electrodynamics (cQED) system consisting of a confined single photon and a single quantum emitter serves as a fundamental block for quantum optics and photonic quantum technologies. The canonical optical mode employed in the conventional cavity quantum electrodynamics features a uniform polarization distribution, leading to the scalar light-matter interaction in most existing experiments. Despite the rapid progress in the generation of structured light with spatially varied polarizations, the structured light-matter interaction, especially at the single quanta level, is highly intriguing yet largely unexplored. Here, we present the structured light-matter interaction at the single-photon level in a semiconductor cavity quantum electrodynamics system. Four distinct structured cavity modes that are spectrally close to each other are constructed in a micropillar cavity. By spatially locating a single epitaxial quantum dot (QD) at the periphery of a semiconductor micropillar cavity and spectrally tuning the QD emission wavelength into the resonances of the structured cavity modes, cavity-enhanced single-photon emissions with spin-locked chiral orbital angular momentum (OAM) and engineerable spin-orbit entanglements are achieved within a single wavelength-scale device. Our work opens an unexplored paradigm of structured quantum light-matter interactions and may further advance chiral quantum optics and high-dimensional photonic quantum technology.
tldr: This paper demonstrates structured light-matter interaction at the single-photon level in a semiconductor cavity QED system, achieving spin-locked chiral OAM and engineerable spin-orbit entanglement.
motivation: Conventional cQED uses scalar modes with uniform polarization; structured light with spatially varying polarization enables new quantum phenomena but has been unexplored at the single-quanta level.
method: The authors construct four distinct structured cavity modes in a micropillar cavity and spatially locate a single quantum dot at the periphery, spectrally tuning it into resonance with the modes.
result: They observe cavity-enhanced single-photon emissions with spin-locked chiral orbital angular momentum and engineerable spin-orbit entanglement within a single device.
conclusion: This work opens a new paradigm of structured quantum light-matter interactions, advancing chiral quantum optics and high-dimensional photonic quantum technologies.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper reports the first experimental demonstration of structured light-matter interaction at the single-photon level in a semiconductor cavity quantum electrodynamics (cQED) system. The authors construct four distinct structured cavity modes with spatially varying polarization within a micropillar cavity, each spectrally close to one another. By positioning a single epitaxial quantum dot (QD) at the periphery of the micropillar and tuning its emission wavelength into resonance with these structured modes, they achieve cavity-enhanced single-photon emission with spin-locked chiral orbital angular momentum (OAM) and engineerable spin-orbit entanglements. The work extends conventional scalar cQED into the realm of structured light, enabling new forms of quantum light-matter interaction within a single wavelength-scale device. The results open avenues for chiral quantum optics and high-dimensional photonic quantum technologies.

Spectral tuning of the QD emission is performed via temperature or electric field control to bring it into resonance with the cavity modes. The emitted single photons are characterized using polarization-resolved and OAM-resolved spectroscopy, as well as second-order correlation measurements to verify single-photon statistics. title: Picosecond-resolved Entanglement Distribution Over An Urban Free-space Channel
authors: Alessandro Laneve, Fabrizio Cienzo, Santiago Gomez, Paolo Barigelli, Philip Menz, Mattia Beccaceci, Giuseppe Ronco, Giorgia Grossi, Ievgen Brytavskyi, Thomas Oberleitner, Markus Wiener, Christian Weidinger, Tobias M. abstract: ArXiv:2607.21093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-evolving entangled states describe quantum particles whose correlations evolve in time according to a well-defined dynamics. Such states can be generated in a variety of physical systems and are promising resources for several quantum technologies, ranging from quantum clock synchronization to quantum communication. However, their full potential is currently limited by the fact that the entanglement dynamics often occur on timescales comparable to the achievable synchronization precision, especially in experiments aimed at distributing entanglement through noisy urban channels. In this context, accurate timing is not merely a technical detail, but a fundamental requirement for faithfully observing and exploiting the underlying quantum correlations. Here, we demonstrate the faithful distribution of a fast-evolving entangled state over a 270 m free-space channel connecting two buildings in the center of Rome. The developed system incorporates a synchronization device capable of achieving sub-50 ps timing accuracy between the two ends of the link while simultaneously supporting channel stabilization. Our results demonstrate that time-evolving entanglement can be reliably transmitted through a noisy urban free-space channel, representing an important benchmark toward long-distance free-space quantum communication and the future implementation of time-correlated entangled states in demanding scenarios such as satellite-based quantum networks.

motivation: Time-evolving entangled states are promising for quantum technologies but their distribution is limited by synchronization precision, especially in noisy urban channels.
method: Developed a free-space entanglement distribution system with a synchronization device achieving sub-50 ps timing accuracy and channel stabilization over a 270 m link between two buildings in Rome.
result: Successfully distributed fast-evolving entangled states through a noisy urban free-space channel, maintaining high-fidelity correlations.
conclusion: This work establishes a benchmark for long-distance free-space quantum communication and supports future satellite-based quantum networks using time-correlated entangled states.
