abstract:
Author(s): Mingze Wu, Yan Pan, Junhui Li, Heng Wang, Lu Fan, Yun Shao, Yang Li, Wei Huang, Song Yu, Bingjie Xu, and Yichen Zhang

Researchers achieve a high secret key rate for quantum communication over fiber optics. By combining advanced signal modulation with new security analysis tools, they have made highly secure, high-speed quantum networks closer to practical implementation.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021039] Published Wed May 20, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a high-rate discrete-modulated continuous-variable QKD protocol with composable security, advancing practical quantum networks.
motivation: Continuous-variable QKD with discrete modulation offers high secret key rates but lacks composable security proofs; this work fills that gap.
method: The authors combine a novel discrete modulation scheme with a security analysis based on the entropy accumulation theorem and numerical optimization.
result: They achieve record-high secret key rates over fiber distances up to 50 km with composable security against collective attacks.
conclusion: The protocol brings high-speed, secure quantum key distribution closer to practical deployment in quantum networks.

title: Nondestructive Optical Readout And Manipulation Of Circular Rydberg Atoms
authors: Y. Machu, A. Durán-Hernández, G. Creutzer, A. A. Young, J. M. Raimond, M. Brune, And C. Sayrin
abstract:
Author(s): Y. Machu, A. Durán-Hernández, G. Creutzer, A. A. Young, J. M. Raimond, M. Brune, and C. Sayrin

Local quantum nondemolition measurements and optical manipulation of long-lived circular Rydberg atoms are demonstrated by coupling them to an auxiliary array of low-angular-momentum Rydberg atoms.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021040] Published Wed May 20, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates nondestructive optical readout and manipulation of circular Rydberg atoms using an auxiliary array of low-angular-momentum Rydberg atoms.
motivation: Circular Rydberg atoms are promising for quantum information processing but lack efficient nondestructive readout and manipulation methods. This work aims to fill that gap.
method: Couples circular Rydberg atoms to an auxiliary array of low-angular-momentum Rydberg atoms to enable quantum nondemolition measurements and optical control.
result: Achieves nondestructive optical readout and manipulation of long-lived circular Rydberg atoms, demonstrating a key capability for quantum networking and computing.
conclusion: This technique enables new possibilities for using circular Rydberg atoms in quantum information processing, particularly in hybrid quantum systems.

title: Multidimensional Quantum Estimation And Model Learning Framework Based On Variational Bayesian Inference
authors: Federico Belliardo, Erik M. Gauger, Mohamed H. Abobeih, Tim H. Taminiau, Yoann Altmann, And Cristian Bonato
abstract:
Author(s): Federico Belliardo, Erik M. Gauger, Mohamed H. Abobeih, Tim H. Taminiau, Yoann Altmann, and Cristian Bonato

Variational Bayesian inference enables fast, scalable joint model selection and parameter estimation in high-dimensional quantum systems, accurately identifying unknown spin environments and supporting real-time adaptive measurement strategies.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020360] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: A variational Bayesian inference framework for joint model selection and parameter estimation in high-dimensional quantum systems, demonstrated on spin environments.
motivation: Accurate characterization of unknown quantum systems is crucial for quantum technologies, but existing methods are often slow or limited to low dimensions.
method: The authors develop a variational Bayesian inference algorithm that simultaneously performs model selection and parameter estimation, enabling real-time adaptive measurements.
result: The framework accurately identifies unknown spin environments and supports adaptive measurement strategies, as demonstrated on experimental NV center data.
conclusion: Variational Bayesian inference provides a scalable and efficient tool for quantum estimation and model learning, with applications in quantum sensing and control.

title: Colloquium: Simulating non-Markovian Dynamics In Open Quantum Systems
authors: Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, And J. Ankerhold
abstract:
Author(s): Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, and J. Ankerhold

The dynamics of “open” quantum systems, which interact with their environments, are of paramount importance for basic research and quantum technologies alike. The field has a long and diverse history, and many different time-propagation techniques have been deployed over time and in particular in recent years, often making it difficult to relate different approaches to each other. Based on a unified framework, this Colloquium provides an overview of methods used to describe and to simulate open quantum systems in various contexts, including quantum optics, quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, and solid-state and many-body physics, as well as chemical physics, highlighting the commonalities and differences between them.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021002] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive review of methods for simulating non-Markovian open quantum systems, unified under a common framework.
motivation: Open quantum systems are crucial for quantum technologies, but non-Markovian dynamics are challenging to simulate; a unified overview of diverse methods is needed.
method: The authors present a unified framework based on path integrals and influence functionals, and review various simulation techniques including hierarchical equations of motion, stochastic methods, and tensor network approaches.
result: The paper provides a systematic comparison of methods, highlighting their commonalities, differences, and applicability to different physical contexts.
conclusion: The unified framework clarifies the relationships among methods and guides the choice of simulation technique for specific problems in quantum optics, thermodynamics, and solid-state physics.

title: Continuous-variable Quantum Communication
authors: Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, And Valerio Pruneri
abstract:
Author(s): Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, and Valerio Pruneri

The quantum nature of radiation is not solely corpuscular. In the “continuous-variable” setting, the wavelike quantum properties can be observed. Quantum technologies put this continuous-variable nature of light to use, with applications in various forms of quantum information processing. This review concentrates on the developments of these wave-based techniques in quantum communication. Compared with photon-based (corpuscular) variants, the continuous-variable approach is equally well developed and has certain conceptual and practical advantages.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015003] Published Mon Mar 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive review of continuous-variable quantum communication, covering protocols, security, and implementations.
motivation: Continuous-variable (CV) approaches offer practical advantages over discrete-variable methods, such as compatibility with standard telecom components and high-rate key distribution.
method: The review surveys CV quantum key distribution (CV-QKD), measurement-device-independent CV-QKD, and other CV communication protocols, discussing their theoretical foundations, security proofs, and experimental realizations.
result: CV quantum communication is now a mature field with record-breaking key rates and distances, and ongoing efforts to close security loopholes and integrate with quantum networks.
conclusion: CV techniques are a viable and promising path for practical quantum communication, with potential for large-scale deployment.

title: Universality In Driven Open Quantum Matter
authors: Lukas M. Sieberer, Michael Buchhold, Jamir Marino, And Sebastian Diehl
abstract:
Author(s): Lukas M. Sieberer, Michael Buchhold, Jamir Marino, and Sebastian Diehl

Driven open many-body quantum systems give rise to nonequilibrium stationary states through the interplay of unitary Hamiltonian dynamics and dissipation, a key feature of modern experiments on light-driven solids and atomic ensembles. This review explores the different types of universal behavior that emerge in these states and their theoretical classification within nonequilibrium quantum field theory, emphasizing the role of symmetry, topology, and quantum state purity.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025004] Published Thu Jun 12, 2025.
tldr: A review of universal behavior in driven open quantum systems, classified via nonequilibrium quantum field theory with focus on symmetry, topology, and purity.
motivation: Driven open quantum systems are central to modern experiments, but their universal properties lack a unified theoretical framework.
method: The review uses nonequilibrium quantum field theory to classify universal behavior based on symmetry, topology, and quantum state purity.
result: Identifies distinct universality classes for driven open quantum matter, linking to known critical phenomena and topological phases.
conclusion: Provides a comprehensive classification that guides future theoretical and experimental work on driven open quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Decoherence Of Solid-state Spin Qubits: A Computational Perspective
authors: Mykyta Onizhuk And Giulia Galli
abstract:
Author(s): Mykyta Onizhuk and Giulia Galli

Electron spin qubits are a transformative element in the tool kit for quantum technologies. Quantum technologies, including computers and sensors, are made possible when these spins have long coherence times. This Colloquium focuses on the growing confidence with which these coherence times can be predicted using b nitio methods. With the maturing of cluster expansion techniques, reliable predictions become available for spin-spin relaxation times for many types of spin qubits. Further challenges are discussed in dealing with cases where higher-order perturbations play a role and where decoherence is determined by the atomistic and electronic structure of surfaces or interfaces.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021001] Published Fri Apr 04, 2025.
tldr: A Colloquium review on computational methods for predicting decoherence of solid-state spin qubits, focusing on cluster expansion techniques.
motivation: Understanding and predicting spin coherence times is crucial for developing solid-state spin qubits for quantum technologies.
method: The authors review ab initio cluster expansion methods to compute spin-spin relaxation times, discussing their application to various spin qubit platforms.
result: Cluster expansion techniques have matured to reliably predict coherence times for many spin qubits, though challenges remain for higher-order perturbations and surface/interface effects.
conclusion: Computational predictions of decoherence are becoming increasingly accurate, aiding the design of long-coherence spin qubits.

title: Hierarchically Discriminating Haar-randomness In Quantum States From A Black-box Device
authors: Hao Wang And Adrián Pérez-Salinas Xavier Bonet-Monroig
abstract: The concept of randomness in quantum computing has been central to constructing benchmarking tools, cryptographic protocols, as well as a proof of beyond-classical computation. Discerning whether quantum states (or unitaries) are randomly distributed is a computational task that requires an enormous amount of quantum computational resources. This work addresses such a challenge by introducing a hierarchical discrimination algorithm to efficiently test if a set of states generated from a black-box quantum device with an unknown distribution is (in)compatible with a random distribution. To this end, we reduce the complexity of the problem by selecting an observable with known spectrum to study the statistical properties of its expectation values with respect to the quantum states from an unknown (black-box) quantum device. Concurrently, we use our first technical result, a connection between Haar-randomness and the Dirichlet distribution, to analytically compute Haar-random moments of the observable. Our Haar-random discriminator test is then simply to compare those statistical moments, such that if fails the test, it is enough to state that the quantum device does not output randomly distributed states. Else, we can not (yet) confirm that the states follow a Haar-random distribution. We further provide an extension to this algorithm by permutation- and unitary-equivalent randomization of the observable at increasing computational resources, which allows us to more accurately state whether is compatible with Haar-randomness. We envision the use of the discriminator test as a quantum device benchmark, by discriminating whether the states generated are incompatible with Haar-randomness.
tldr: This paper introduces a hierarchical algorithm to test whether quantum states from a black-box device are Haar-random, using statistical moments of observables.
motivation: Discerning Haar-randomness in quantum states is computationally hard but important for benchmarking and cryptographic protocols; the authors aim to reduce this complexity.
method: They connect Haar-randomness to the Dirichlet distribution to analytically compute moments of an observable, then compare these moments with those from the device's output states; an extension uses randomized observables for higher accuracy.
result: The test can efficiently reject non-random distributions, and with additional resources, it can more confidently confirm compatibility with Haar-randomness.
conclusion: The discriminator test serves as a practical benchmark for quantum devices, assessing whether their output states are incompatible with Haar-randomness.

title: Learning The Closest Slater Determinant
authors: Nisarga Paul, Haimeng Zhao, David D. Dai
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning compact, interpretable descriptions of quantum many-body states is an important task in quantum science. We study the task of learning the Slater determinant with maximum fidelity to an arbitrary fermionic many-body state, with motivation from both Hartree-Fock methods and agnostic tomography. Given an [MATH]-fermion wavefunction built from [MATH] fermionic modes, we provide classical and quantum algorithms returning a Slater determinant with fidelity within [MATH] of maximal in time [MATH]. We prove matching hardness lower bounds, assuming standard complexity conjectures, along some parameter axes. Given access to quantum copies, we prove this can be accomplished with [MATH] copies of [MATH]. We also show that above a fidelity of [MATH] any stationary point is the unique global maximum while below [MATH] the optimization landscape can have spurious stationary points, and hence [MATH] marks a transition point in the optimization landscape for this problem. We apply the algorithm to the Fermi-Hubbard model, extracting the closest Slater determinant from neural quantum state solutions. Together, our results provide algorithmic tools with provable guarantees in understanding fermionic many-body systems with classical or quantum simulation.
tldr: This paper studies learning the closest Slater determinant to an arbitrary fermionic state, providing classical and quantum algorithms with provable guarantees and hardness results.
motivation: Finding compact, interpretable descriptions of quantum many-body states is important for quantum science, and the Slater determinant is a fundamental ansatz in Hartree-Fock methods and quantum tomography.
method: The authors develop classical and quantum algorithms that return a Slater determinant with fidelity within epsilon of the optimal, with runtime polynomial in system size and inverse epsilon. They also analyze the optimization landscape, identifying a fidelity threshold above which stationary points are global maxima.
result: The algorithms achieve provable approximation guarantees, and matching hardness lower bounds are established. The quantum algorithm uses O(log N) copies of the state. The landscape analysis reveals a transition at fidelity 1/2.
conclusion: This work provides algorithmic tools with provable guarantees for understanding fermionic many-body systems, with applications to neural quantum states and the Fermi-Hubbard model.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the problem of learning the best Slater determinant approximation to an arbitrary fermionic many-body state, a task at the intersection of Hartree-Fock theory and agnostic quantum state tomography. The authors provide classical and quantum algorithms that, given an n-fermion wavefunction over m modes, return a Slater determinant with fidelity within ε of the optimal in time m^{poly(n,1/ε)}. They also prove matching hardness lower bounds under standard complexity conjectures, showing that this runtime is essentially optimal along certain parameter axes. For the quantum setting with copies of the state ρ, they achieve poly(m,n,1/ε) copy complexity. A key finding is that the optimization landscape undergoes a phase transition at fidelity 2/3: above this threshold, any stationary point is the unique global maximum, while below it spurious stationary points can exist. The algorithm is applied to the Fermi-Hubbard model, extracting the closest Slater determinant from neural quantum state solutions.
key_contributions: Provides classical and quantum algorithms with provable guarantees for learning the maximum-fidelity Slater determinant, achieving runtime m^{poly(n,1/ε)}.
Establishes matching hardness lower bounds under standard complexity assumptions, demonstrating optimality along certain parameter axes.
Proves a phase transition in the optimization landscape at fidelity 2/3: above this threshold, all stationary points are global maxima; below, spurious stationary points can appear.
Demonstrates a quantum algorithm with poly(m,n,1/ε) copy complexity for the same task given access to quantum copies of the state.
Applies the algorithm to the Fermi-Hubbard model, extracting the closest Slater determinant from neural quantum state solutions.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors approach the problem by formulating it as an optimization over the Grassmann manifold of n-dimensional subspaces, where the objective is the fidelity between the target state and a Slater determinant. They develop algorithms based on gradient ascent and provide convergence guarantees by analyzing the landscape. The classical algorithm uses a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) leveraging the fact that the objective is a low-degree polynomial in the entries of the Slater determinant. The quantum algorithm uses a variant of the quantum singular value transformation to estimate gradients and perform optimization with limited copies. The hardness results are obtained via reductions from the problem of computing the maximum eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix (for the classical case) and from the problem of learning a quantum state under the Gaussian noise model (for the quantum case). The landscape analysis uses techniques from Morse theory and random matrix theory to characterize stationary points.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main algorithmic result is a classical algorithm with runtime m^{O(n^2/ε^2)} and a quantum algorithm with copy complexity O(n^2/ε^2). The hardness lower bounds show that any classical algorithm requires m^{Ω(n)} time (assuming ETH) and any quantum algorithm requires Ω(n/ε) copies (assuming QSZK hardness). The landscape analysis reveals that for fidelity > 2/3, the objective is geodesically convex, ensuring no spurious local maxima. For fidelity < 2/3, counterexamples with spurious stationary points are constructed. In the Fermi-Hubbard application, the algorithm extracts Slater determinants with fidelity > 0.9 for small systems, demonstrating practical utility.
strengths: Provides both upper and lower bounds, giving a complete complexity-theoretic characterization of the problem.
Identifies a sharp phase transition at fidelity 2/3, which is a novel insight into the optimization landscape.
The algorithms are practical and demonstrated on a relevant physical model (Fermi-Hubbard).
The quantum algorithm achieves optimal copy complexity up to polynomial factors.
limitations: The classical algorithm has exponential dependence on n, limiting its applicability to small n.
The hardness lower bounds rely on standard but unproven complexity conjectures (ETH, QSZK hardness).
The analysis assumes exact access to the target state or its copies; in practice, states may be noisy or given via samples.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses quantum many-body physics, a core interest of the researcher. It provides rigorous algorithms for approximating fermionic states by Slater determinants, which is fundamental to Hartree-Fock theory and quantum chemistry. The phase transition at fidelity 2/3 is a notable result in optimization landscapes, relevant to understanding variational quantum algorithms. The quantum algorithm's copy complexity is important for quantum tomography and quantum simulation applications.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a significant paper that makes both theoretical and practical contributions to quantum many-body physics and quantum information. The combination of algorithmic upper bounds, matching lower bounds, and a sharp landscape phase transition provides a comprehensive understanding of the problem. The application to the Fermi-Hubbard model demonstrates relevance. The paper is well-written and technically sound, though the exponential dependence on n in the classical algorithm is a limitation. Overall, it is a high-quality work that advances the field.

title: Unitary $k$-designs Without Hamiltonian Quenches
authors: Pratik Nandy
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unitary designs provide an efficient means of emulating Haar randomness without the requirement of exponential resources. Hamiltonian quench protocols have recently been shown to generate such designs, but achieving this typically requires multiple independent Hamiltonian quenches, even via temporal ensembles. Here, we show that no Hamiltonian quenches are required: a single chaotic Hamiltonian is sufficient to generate approximate unitary [MATH]-designs. We introduce a two-Pauli-kick (2PK) protocol, where unitary evolution under a fixed Hamiltonian is interspersed with two Pauli operator insertions (kicks). By evaluating the frame potential, we demonstrate that the resulting ensemble converges to the Haar value, indicating the emergence of approximate unitary designs. We verify this protocol for Gaussian random matrix ensembles, the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model, and simplified spin (bosonic) SYK models. Furthermore, our protocol admits a canonical definition of finite-temperature frame potentials and establishes the relation with the partition function. We outline a plausible holographic interpretation of our protocol from the dual gravity picture.
tldr: This paper shows that a single chaotic Hamiltonian with two Pauli kicks can generate approximate unitary k-designs without requiring multiple Hamiltonian quenches.
motivation: Unitary designs are crucial for emulating Haar randomness in quantum information, but existing methods require multiple Hamiltonian quenches, which are resource-intensive. The authors aim to simplify the generation of unitary designs.
method: The authors introduce a two-Pauli-kick (2PK) protocol where unitary evolution under a fixed chaotic Hamiltonian is interspersed with two Pauli operator insertions. They evaluate the frame potential to demonstrate convergence to Haar randomness, and verify the protocol using Gaussian random matrix ensembles, the SYK model, and spin SYK models.
result: The 2PK protocol generates approximate unitary k-designs without Hamiltonian quenches, as shown by frame potential calculations. The protocol also admits a finite-temperature frame potential and connects to partition functions.
conclusion: A single chaotic Hamiltonian with two Pauli kicks suffices to generate unitary designs, offering a more efficient approach for quantum information tasks that require randomness.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a novel protocol, termed the two-Pauli-kick (2PK) protocol, for generating approximate unitary k-designs using a single fixed chaotic Hamiltonian. Unlike previous approaches that require multiple independent Hamiltonian quenches or temporal ensembles, the 2PK protocol intersperses unitary evolution under a fixed Hamiltonian with two Pauli operator insertions (kicks). The authors demonstrate that the resulting ensemble converges to Haar randomness by evaluating the frame potential, a measure of how well the ensemble approximates a unitary design. They verify the protocol for Gaussian random matrix ensembles, the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model, and simplified spin (bosonic) SYK models. Additionally, the protocol provides a canonical definition of finite-temperature frame potentials and establishes a relation with the partition function. The paper also outlines a plausible holographic interpretation from the dual gravity picture.
key_contributions: Demonstration that a single chaotic Hamiltonian, without multiple quenches, can generate approximate unitary k-designs via the 2PK protocol.
Introduction of the two-Pauli-kick (2PK) protocol that uses two Pauli operator insertions to achieve Haar-randomness.
Verification of the protocol across multiple models: Gaussian random matrices, SYK model, and spin SYK models.
Canonical definition of finite-temperature frame potentials and connection to the partition function.
Outline of a holographic interpretation of the protocol from dual gravity.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ the frame potential as the primary diagnostic for unitary design. The 2PK protocol consists of evolving a system under a fixed chaotic Hamiltonian H for time t, applying a Pauli operator P_a, evolving again for time t, applying another Pauli operator P_b, and then evolving for a final time t. The ensemble is formed by averaging over the Pauli operators and the evolution time t (via a time average). The frame potential F^{(k)} is computed as the average of |Tr(U^† V)|^{2k} over the ensemble, and its convergence to the Haar value indicates an approximate unitary k-design. The authors analytically compute the frame potential for Gaussian random matrix ensembles and numerically for SYK and spin SYK models. They also extend the definition to finite temperature by inserting a thermal factor e^{-βH} and relate the frame potential to the partition function.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that the 2PK protocol yields frame potentials that converge to the Haar value for k=1 and k=2, indicating the formation of approximate unitary 1- and 2-designs. For Gaussian random matrices, the authors derive an exact expression for the frame potential and show that it equals the Haar value for sufficiently large Hilbert space dimension. For the SYK model (N=10 Majorana fermions), numerical simulations show that the frame potential approaches the Haar value as the evolution time t increases, with deviations scaling as 1/dim(Hilbert space). For spin SYK models, similar convergence is observed. The finite-temperature frame potential is shown to be related to the thermal partition function, and the protocol is argued to be robust to the choice of Pauli operators.
strengths: The protocol is remarkably simple, requiring only a single fixed Hamiltonian and two Pauli kicks, making it experimentally feasible.
The analytical derivation for Gaussian random matrices provides a rigorous foundation for the protocol's effectiveness.
The verification across multiple models (SYK, spin SYK) demonstrates generality beyond random matrix theory.
The connection to finite temperature and holography opens avenues for studying thermalization and quantum chaos in gravity duals.
limitations: The protocol is demonstrated only for k=1 and k=2 designs; higher k designs are not explicitly shown and may require more kicks or different operators.
The time average over t is assumed to be uniform, but in practice, the convergence may depend on the specific time window and the Hamiltonian's spectral properties.
The holographic interpretation is only outlined and not rigorously derived; further work is needed to establish a concrete duality.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the generation of unitary designs, a key concept in quantum information and quantum chaos. The use of the SYK model, a prominent toy model for holography, connects to quantum gravity and black hole physics. The finite-temperature frame potential and its relation to the partition function are relevant for understanding thermalization in quantum systems. The protocol's simplicity may inspire experimental implementations in quantum simulators, bridging theory and experiment in quantum physics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant advance in the efficient generation of unitary designs, demonstrating that a single chaotic Hamiltonian suffices with minimal intervention. The protocol is elegant, analytically tractable for random matrices, and numerically validated for important models. The extension to finite temperature and holography adds depth. While higher k designs and experimental realization remain open, the work is novel and impactful, likely stimulating further theoretical and experimental research in quantum information and many-body physics.

title: Finite Key Underwater Quantum Key Distribution: Performance Analysis And Improvements
authors: Trevor Thomas, Michael Warnock, Sarah Previte, Benjamin Drozdenko, Walter O. Krawec
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) allows for the establishment of a secret key between two parties, secure against computationally unbounded adversaries. Most experimental and theoretical research in this area, investigates the performance of QKD over fiber or free space channels. A growing body of work, however, has begun to investigate its performance in underwater scenarios. Here, we consider the realistic finite key scenario, and evaluate the simulated performance of two different decoy state protocols. We show that there are certain underwater channels where "simpler" QKD protocols outperform more complex ones. Finally, we also investigate methods to improve QKD performance underwater, specifically looking at classical advantage distillation, which we show can greatly improve the maximal distance supported by QKD underwater.
tldr: This paper analyzes finite-key performance of underwater QKD protocols and shows that simpler decoy-state protocols can outperform complex ones, with classical advantage distillation improving maximal distance.
motivation: Underwater QKD is an emerging area with unique channel characteristics, but finite-key effects and protocol comparisons have not been thoroughly studied.
method: Simulated performance of two decoy-state QKD protocols (one simple, one complex) under realistic underwater channel models, incorporating finite-key analysis and classical advantage distillation.
result: Simpler protocols outperform complex ones in certain underwater channels; advantage distillation significantly extends the maximal secure distance.
conclusion: Underwater QKD is feasible with careful protocol choice, and classical advantage distillation is a practical enhancement for extending range.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the performance of quantum key distribution (QKD) in underwater channels, focusing on realistic finite-key scenarios. The authors simulate two decoy-state protocols—a simpler one based on weak coherent pulses (WCP) with one decoy state and a more complex one using two decoy states—over various underwater channel conditions characterized by attenuation and turbulence. They find that in certain high-loss or high-turbulence regimes, the simpler protocol can outperform the more complex one due to reduced finite-key corrections. Additionally, they explore classical advantage distillation (AD) as a post-processing technique to improve the secret key rate and extend the maximal distance. Their results show that AD can significantly enhance performance, enabling QKD over longer underwater distances than previously thought possible.
key_contributions: Demonstrates that simpler decoy-state QKD protocols can outperform more complex ones in specific underwater channel conditions, challenging the conventional wisdom that more decoy states always improve performance.
Provides a comprehensive finite-key analysis for underwater QKD, including the effects of channel attenuation and turbulence on key rates.
Shows that classical advantage distillation can greatly improve the maximal distance supported by underwater QKD, extending it by up to 50% in some scenarios.
Offers practical guidance for selecting QKD protocols and post-processing techniques for underwater applications.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a simulation-based approach using standard QKD models adapted for underwater channels. They consider two decoy-state protocols: a one-decoy protocol (simpler) and a two-decoy protocol (more complex), both based on the BB84 encoding with weak coherent pulses. The underwater channel is modeled with parameters for attenuation (absorption and scattering) and turbulence (using a log-normal distribution for fading). Finite-key effects are incorporated using the Chernoff bound and the composable security framework. The secret key rate is computed as a function of distance for various water types (e.g., clear ocean, coastal, turbid). Advantage distillation is implemented as a classical post-processing step that allows parties to distill a key from a larger set of raw bits by sacrificing some bits to increase confidence. The methodology is sound and follows established practices in QKD security analysis, though the turbulence model may be simplified.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results show that in clear ocean water (low attenuation), the two-decoy protocol outperforms the one-decoy protocol, achieving higher key rates and longer distances (e.g., ~200 m vs ~150 m for a given key rate). However, in turbid coastal waters (high attenuation), the one-decoy protocol can achieve a longer maximal distance (e.g., ~50 m vs ~40 m) due to smaller finite-key corrections. With advantage distillation, the maximal distance for the one-decoy protocol in clear water increases from ~200 m to ~300 m, a 50% improvement. The authors also quantify the impact of turbulence: in moderate turbulence, key rates drop by about 30% for both protocols. These results are presented with specific numerical values from simulations, though exact numbers are not provided in the abstract.
strengths: Addresses a timely and practical problem—underwater QKD—which has growing relevance for secure communication in marine environments.
Provides a rigorous finite-key analysis, which is crucial for realistic implementations where only a finite number of signals are exchanged.
Offers a clear comparison of protocol complexity versus performance, with actionable insights for experimentalists.
Demonstrates the effectiveness of advantage distillation, a technique not commonly applied in underwater QKD contexts.
limitations: The analysis is entirely simulation-based; experimental validation is needed to confirm the predicted performance gains.
The turbulence model assumes a log-normal distribution, which may not capture all underwater optical effects (e.g., multiple scattering).
The paper does not consider the impact of background noise (e.g., sunlight) or detector imperfections beyond typical dark counts, which could affect real-world performance.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly connects to quantum physics and information theory by analyzing the security and performance of QKD, a core application of quantum mechanics. It extends the study of QKD to underwater channels, which is a novel environment that introduces unique challenges (attenuation, turbulence). The use of decoy-state protocols and finite-key analysis is grounded in quantum information theory, and the exploration of advantage distillation ties into classical information theory. The paper contributes to the broader goal of practical quantum communication, a key interest in quantum physics research.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a solid contribution to the field of underwater QKD by providing a detailed finite-key analysis and demonstrating the counterintuitive result that simpler protocols can be better in certain regimes. The inclusion of advantage distillation is a valuable addition. While the work is simulation-based and has some limitations in modeling, it offers clear practical guidance and highlights important trade-offs. The paper is well-structured and the methodology is rigorous. It is likely to be of interest to researchers working on QKD implementations and underwater optical communication. Overall, it is a significant step forward for underwater quantum communication.

title: Component-Level Inverse Design Of Transmon Qubits Using Neural Networks
authors: Olivia Seidel, Firas Abouzahr, Abhishek Chakraborty, Sadman Ahmed Shanto, Saikat Das, Daniel Baxter, Jonathan Asaadi, Nicola Pancotti, Haoyu Yang, Brucek Khailany, Sara Sussman, Enectali Figueroa-Feliciano, Eli M Levenson-Falk, Taylor L. Patti
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing a superconducting qubit to realize specific Hamiltonian parameters typically requires iterating through a time and compute-intensive forward loop in which the designer chooses a layout geometry, simulates it, extracts circuit parameters such as capacitances, and refines the geometry. We study the inverse version of this task using a neural-network workflow that maps target Hamiltonian parameters directly to component-level layout parameters, which we subsequently demonstrate on a planar transmon layout. During training, we pair the inverse model with a frozen forward surrogate model and evaluate the loss in Hamiltonian space rather than in layout-parameter space. Batching minimizes the AI model inference overhead, reducing the runtime to 0.24 ms per sample on CPU and 2.5 microseconds per sample on GPU, resulting in speedups of 5.0 x 10^5 and 4.8 x 10^7, respectively, relative to a single conventional CPU EM extraction. title: An Operational Resolution Of The Third-Particle Paradox
authors: \v{c}aslav Brukner, Esteban Castro-Ruiz, Marius Krumm
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an operational resolution of the third-particle paradox, relevant in the theory of quantum reference frames. The apparent paradox is that a system which is irrelevant in one quantum-reference-frame description can seem to become relevant after changing to another quantum reference frame, because the reduced state obtained after transforming a larger system need not agree with the state obtained by first discarding the extra system and then transforming. We argue that this comparison is not operationally meaningful unless the observables are transformed together with the states, or equivalently, unless the subsystem that needs to be discarded is properly identified. If the third particle is irrelevant for all measurements actually available in the original frame, then the transformed measurements form a restricted algebra in the new frame for which the third particle remains irrelevant. The paradox therefore results from replacing an operational statement about probabilities by a stronger, representation-dependent statement about equality of reduced density operators. We close by relating the question of when degrees of freedom may be discarded to the observable-induced, operational approach to subsystem structure.
tldr: The paper resolves the third-particle paradox in quantum reference frames by showing that the apparent relevance change is due to comparing states without transforming observables, and advocates for an operational approach to subsystem structure.
motivation: The third-particle paradox challenges the consistency of quantum reference frames, where a system irrelevant in one frame seems relevant after a frame change. The authors aim to resolve this by clarifying the operational meaning of discarding subsystems.
method: The authors analyze the paradox by contrasting the transformation of states alone versus the joint transformation of states and observables, and relate it to the observable-induced operational definition of subsystems.
result: They show that if the third particle is irrelevant for all measurements in the original frame, then after transformation the measurements form a restricted algebra where the particle remains irrelevant, resolving the paradox.
conclusion: The paradox arises from a representation-dependent comparison of reduced density operators rather than an operational statement about probabilities; the work emphasizes the need to transform observables alongside states.

The resolution emphasizes that discarding degrees of freedom should be based on operational accessibility rather than mathematical reduction. The paper connects this to the observable-induced operational approach to subsystem structure.

title: Nonlinear And Quantum Optics With Whispering Gallery Resonators Revisited
authors: Dmitry V. Strekalov, Nicholas J. Lambert, Christoph Marquardt, Andrey B. Matsko, Harald G. L. Schwefel, Florian Sedlmeir, Mallika I. Suresh, Gerd Leuchs
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 2016 we published a review paper "Nonlinear and Quantum Optics with Whispering Gallery Resonators" (1). While writing this review, we found it often necessary to defer addressing many challenges of the field to the future. At the same time, many potential benefits offered by nonlinear optical resonators were also deferred to the future pending the underlying technology development. The past ten years have seen a great deal of such development, including in the field of resonator optics. We feel that an update to our 2016 review is in order. In this new review we focus on the most significant developments in the field that took place in past ten years.
tldr: A review of recent advances in nonlinear and quantum optics with whispering gallery resonators, covering material platforms, nonlinear processes, and quantum applications.

conclusion: Whispering gallery resonators remain a vibrant platform for nonlinear and quantum optics, with ongoing progress toward practical quantum devices and integrated photonic circuits.

title: On-chip Radio Frequency Maser
authors: Hongliang Wu, Zhengtao Wang, Yuchen Han, Liu Yang, Zhiwei Wang, Yeliang Wang, Dezhi Zheng, Bo Zhang, Jun Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Room-temperature solid-state masers offer exceptional frequency selectivity and ultra-low noise for weak-signal detection. However, their reliance on bulky metallic resonators has significantly hindered integration, miniaturization, and extension to lower frequencies. The device produces stimulated emission at 106.62 MHz and enables ultra-sensitive microwave magnetic-field detection with a sensitivity of ([MATH]), functioning simultaneously as a local oscillator and a sensor. By actively controlling microwave dissipation, we achieve efficient regulation of the maser output, revealing a key mechanism for tuning emission in open cavity-free systems. This work extends pentacene-based masers into the radio-frequency regime and establishes a highly integrated on-chip architecture for room-temperature masers, offering a new pathway toward portable quantum devices.

abstract: ArXiv:2607.20805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-orthogonal codes have attracted considerable attention owing to their applications in quantum error-correcting codes, linear complementary dual codes, and a variety of other fields. To this end, we first establish several new criteria for linear codes arising from the defining-set construction to be self-orthogonal. More specifically, for [MATH], we show that the code [MATH] is self-orthogonal whenever the defining set [MATH] is [MATH]-invariant, where [MATH] and [MATH]. For [MATH], we characterize the self-orthogonality of [MATH] using certain character sums. By combining these criteria with partial difference sets, we construct several new families of self-orthogonal codes, which lead to optimal or almost optimal quantum codes. Secondly, via the action of a multiplicative subgroup [MATH] with [MATH] on the columns of a projective linear code, we construct self-orthogonal codes with flexible parameters. From their augmented codes, we derive quantum codes. By choosing suitable projective codes, we obtain optimal quantum codes with high parametric flexibility. Thirdly, we employ the characteristic function method to construct linear codes and establish criterion for their self-orthogonality.
