Here, in contrast, we reveal that symmetry breaking can instead en…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033076] Published Fri Jul 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies symmetry breaking in nonlocal metasurfaces, showing that it can enhance confinement and Q-factors, contrary to conventional wisdom.
motivation: To challenge the common belief that symmetry breaking in photonic systems leads to weaker confinement and lower Q-factors.
method: The authors analyze Mie-tronics supermodes in nonlocal metasurfaces, using theoretical modeling and numerical simulations to study the effect of symmetry breaking on mode confinement and quality factors.
result: They find that symmetry breaking can actually enhance confinement and increase Q-factors, enabling supermode formation with improved performance.
conclusion: Symmetry breaking in nonlocal metasurfaces can be exploited to achieve stronger confinement and higher Q-factors, offering new design principles for photonic devices.

title: Inhibition Of Explosive Transitions In Spreading Dynamics By Nonlinear Higher-order Adaptation
authors: Longzhao Liu, Hongwei Zheng, Zhihao Han, Xin Wang, And Shaoting Tang
abstract:
Author(s): Longzhao Liu, Hongwei Zheng, Zhihao Han, Xin Wang, and Shaoting Tang

The coevolution of structure and dynamics, known as adaptation, is a fundamental property in various systems and drives diverse emergent behaviors. However, the adaptation in most works primarily stems from pairwise situations, which is insufficient to capture ubiquitous higher-order characteristics…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033068] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies explosive transitions in spreading dynamics on higher-order networks with nonlinear adaptation, which is unrelated to quantum information theory.
motivation: Understanding how higher-order interactions and nonlinear adaptation affect explosive transitions in spreading dynamics.
method: The authors develop a model of spreading dynamics on simplicial complexes with nonlinear adaptation rules and analyze it using mean-field theory and numerical simulations.
result: Nonlinear higher-order adaptation can inhibit explosive transitions, leading to continuous phase transitions instead.
conclusion: Higher-order interactions and nonlinear adaptation play a crucial role in shaping collective dynamics, offering insights for controlling spreading processes.

title: Colloquium: What Do We Mean By ‘active Matter’?
authors: Michael Te Vrugt, Benno Liebchen, And Michael E. Cates
abstract:
Author(s): Michael te Vrugt, Benno Liebchen, and Michael E. Cates

Active matter has become a lively topic in recent years, but what exactly is meant by the term ‘active matter’ is often unclear. This Colloquium discusses the scientific and semantic issues underlying this ambiguity, as well as the history of the field, and offers a definition of active matter as a well-defined subset of nonequilibrium systems. It then surveys recent developments including nonreciprocal interactions, intracellular phase separation, and quantum active matter.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 031001] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium discusses the definition, history, and recent developments of active matter, a subset of nonequilibrium systems.
motivation: The term 'active matter' is often used ambiguously; the paper aims to clarify its meaning and scope.
method: The authors review the history of the field, propose a definition, and survey recent topics including nonreciprocal interactions, intracellular phase separation, and quantum active matter.
result: A clear definition of active matter is provided, and connections to quantum active matter are briefly discussed.
conclusion: Active matter is a well-defined subset of nonequilibrium systems, but the paper does not present new technical results in quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Tip-enhanced Molecular Fluorescence Microscopy With Atomic-scale Resolution
authors: Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, And Guillaume Schull
abstract:
Author(s): Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, and Guillaume Schull

Scanning probe techniques have transformed our ability to study materials at the atomic scale, providing atom-by-atom views of surfaces. Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy combines scanning probes with optical fluorescence. Such optical techniques normally have spatial resolution limited by the wavelength of the light used. However, using the scanning tip itself as a nanoscale optical antenna confines the electromagnetic field to the tip apex, achieving superresolution down to the atomic scale. Fluorescence is a fundamental probe of materials that reveals electronic structure and vibronic properties by exciting electrons to higher levels and observing the photons emitted when they relax. These capabilities are of particular interest for studying and identifying molecules, submolecular structures, and their reactions. This review discusses the techniques of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy and the new insights they have revealed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025007] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This review discusses tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy achieving atomic-scale resolution using scanning probe techniques.
motivation: To overcome the diffraction limit in optical microscopy and achieve atomic-scale spatial resolution for studying molecular electronic and vibronic properties.
method: Combines scanning tunneling microscopy with a nanoscale optical antenna at the tip apex to confine the electromagnetic field and enhance fluorescence.
result: Achieves superresolution down to the atomic scale, enabling the study of individual molecules and submolecular structures.
conclusion: Tip-enhanced fluorescence microscopy provides a powerful tool for nanoscale optical imaging and spectroscopy of molecules.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational-wave and X-ray measurements.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities found in neutron stars, which is not directly related to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: Review of observational data from gravitational-wave events and X-ray pulse profiles, compared to nuclear equation of state calculations.
result: Constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities are summarized.
conclusion: Future observations will further constrain the equation of state, but the paper does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: This review covers three real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the review aims to showcase how scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy can be combined to characterize such disorder.
method: The authors review applications of scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy to compound semiconductors, emphasizing cases where multiple techniques are combined.
result: The review demonstrates that combining these real-space techniques provides a more complete picture of atomic-scale defects and disorder in semiconductors.
conclusion: Real-space microscopy techniques are powerful for characterizing atomic-scale disorder, and their combination yields deeper insights into semiconductor materials.

title: Ghost Mechanism: An Analytical Model Of Abrupt Learning In Recurrent Networks
authors: Fatih Dinc, Ege Cirakman, Bariscan Kurtkaya, Mert Yuksekgonul, Yiqi Jiang, Mark J. Schnitzer, And Hidenori Tanaka
abstract:
Author(s): Fatih Dinc, Ege Cirakman, Bariscan Kurtkaya, Mert Yuksekgonul, Yiqi Jiang, Mark J. Schnitzer, and Hidenori Tanaka

This study establishes the ghost mechanism as an underlying mechanism for abrupt learning, whereby the recurrent neural network develops ghost points—transient dynamical bottlenecks—and identifies ways to overcome the training instabilities.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021058] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a ghost mechanism in recurrent neural networks to explain abrupt learning, but it is unrelated to quantum information theory or quantum thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding abrupt learning in recurrent neural networks is important for machine learning, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors develop an analytical model of ghost points as transient dynamical bottlenecks in recurrent networks.
result: They identify ghost points as a mechanism for abrupt learning and propose ways to overcome training instabilities.
conclusion: The ghost mechanism provides insight into learning dynamics in recurrent networks, but the work is purely in machine learning and not relevant to the user's research interests.

title: Digitally Programmable Photochromic Hydrogel Contact Lenses As Light-Adaptive Artificial Irises
authors: Asad Nauman, Tristen Moncada, Guli Gulinihali, Muhammad Waleed Khalid, Yeshaiahu Fainman, Abdoulaye Ndao
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Excessive exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation is associated with a range of ocular pathologies, motivating the development of soft optical devices that can dynamically regulate incident light. In the human eye, this adaptive optical functionality is performed by the iris, which modulates pupil size to control retinal irradiance in response to ambient illumination. Here we present a photochromic contact lens based artificial iris that mimics this biological light-adaptation mechanism through reversible, spatially programmable modulation of optical transmission with intrinsic UV blocking. Photochromic dyes are embedded within a biocompatible hydrogel matrix, while the cross-linked network is patterned using a digital micromirror device (DMD)based grayscale UV lithography to encode controlled radial gradients in dye switching. This approach generates iris-like attenuation profiles that emulate pupil-dependent light regulation while enabling customizable iris geometries and transmission patterns. The resulting lenses exhibit rapid and reversible UV-induced darkening with position-dependent kinetics, enabling continuous modulation of transmitted light. The photoresponse remains stable over repeated activation cycles without measurable fatigue. The patterned lenses maintain mechanical stability, controlled swelling, and wettability suitable for contact lens applications. This platform combines programmable photochromism and hydrogel optics to enable light-adaptive lenses that mimic key functions of the human iris.
tldr: This paper presents a photochromic hydrogel contact lens that mimics the human iris for adaptive UV light regulation.
motivation: Excessive UV exposure causes ocular pathologies, motivating the development of soft optical devices that dynamically regulate incident light like the human iris.
method: Photochromic dyes are embedded in a biocompatible hydrogel matrix and patterned using DMD-based grayscale UV lithography to create radial gradients in dye switching, enabling programmable iris-like attenuation profiles.
result: The lenses exhibit rapid, reversible UV-induced darkening with position-dependent kinetics, stable over repeated cycles, and maintain mechanical stability and wettability suitable for contact lens applications.
conclusion: This platform combines programmable photochromism and hydrogel optics to create light-adaptive lenses that mimic key functions of the human iris, with potential for ocular protection and customizable optical devices.

title: Design And Optimization Of Metasurfaces For Silicon Photonics: PhD Thesis
authors: Mathys Le Grand
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metasurfaces, two-dimensional arrangements of subwavelength nanopillars, provide local control over the phase of light, enabling flat optical functions beyond conventional refractive components. Their inverse design, finding the pillar distribution producing a target response, faces two obstacles: the immense dimensionality of the design space and the prohibitive cost of rigorous electromagnetic simulations, precluding exhaustive exploration at device scale. This thesis addresses the challenge in three stages. The first assesses the reliability of rigorous Maxwell solvers: comparing three implementations of Li's factorization rules for RCWA shows that spectral convergence does not guarantee physical fidelity, as these rules implicitly distort the simulated permittivity, most severely in the plasmonic regime. FDTD, immune to such artifacts, is retained as ground truth throughout. The second stage removes the computational bottleneck: a local phase-approximation model, then fully convolutional surrogates trained on FDTD simulations of large pillar metasurfaces, predict the near field almost instantaneously. Exploiting problem symmetries quadruples the training database, and the surrogates generalize to much larger apertures while remaining differentiable. The third stage benchmarks three strategies under a common FDTD protocol ([MATH] between realized and target far fields): Gerchberg-Saxton retrieval and Local Model ([MATH]), surrogate-based and heuristic-initialized gradient descent ([MATH]), and a generative framework based on diffusion models and Schr\"odinger bridges. Hybrid posterior sampling and amplitude constraints restore scale-invariant fidelity on surfaces over 230 times larger than training, with diverse, fabrication-tolerant designs. Database enhancement lifts every approach to [MATH].
tldr: This PhD thesis focuses on the design and optimization of metasurfaces for silicon photonics using inverse design and machine learning surrogates.
motivation: Metasurface design faces high-dimensional optimization and prohibitive simulation costs; the thesis aims to develop efficient computational methods.
method: The author compares RCWA and FDTD solvers, builds convolutional surrogate models trained on FDTD data, and benchmarks Gerchberg-Saxton, gradient descent, and diffusion-based generative frameworks.
result: Surrogate-based gradient descent and diffusion models achieve high fidelity on large metasurfaces, with hybrid posterior sampling enabling scale-invariant design.
conclusion: The proposed methods enable efficient, fabrication-tolerant metasurface design for silicon photonics.

title: Reassessment Of Line Profile Asymmetry In Measurements Of The 1s-2s Energy Interval In Hydrogen
authors: D. Solovyev, A. Anikin, T. Zalialiutdinov, L. Labzowsky
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Experiments to determine transition frequencies in the hydrogen atom represent some of the most precise spectroscopic measurements and are at a higher level among simple atomic systems. The most persistent measured value in hydrogen is the energy interval corresponding to the [MATH] two-photon transition. The achieved experimental precision is several parts of [MATH] and has not changed over the last two decades. Although repeated experiments in 2011 and 2013 have improved the accuracy by several times, the frequency value has not changed significantly. On this basis, the frequency of the [MATH] transition holds pivotal for determining physical quantities such as the Rydberg constant and the proton charge radius. Theoretical efforts to study in detail the effects that might influence such precise measurements have not revealed significant contributions. The present work revises the theoretical analysis of the line contour asymmetry and its influence on the determination of the two-photon absorption transition frequency, taking into account the theoretical achievements of recent years in this direction. It is shown that the asymmetry of the observed profile can lead to a [MATH] transition frequency shift at the level of modern experimental accuracy. The found frequency shift is consistent with the line shape model contribution that forms the error budget of the experimental measurements. Adjustment can be carried out on the basis of the asymmetric profile that has become standard in recent years.
tldr: This paper revises the theoretical analysis of line profile asymmetry in hydrogen 1s-2s transition frequency measurements, finding a shift at the level of modern experimental accuracy.
motivation: The 1s-2s transition frequency in hydrogen is crucial for determining the Rydberg constant and proton charge radius, but theoretical contributions to line asymmetry have not been fully accounted for.
method: The authors perform a detailed theoretical analysis of the line contour asymmetry, incorporating recent theoretical advances to compute the frequency shift due to asymmetric line profiles.
result: The asymmetry of the observed profile can lead to a transition frequency shift consistent with the error budget of experimental measurements.
conclusion: Adjustments to the measured frequency can be made using the asymmetric profile model, which has become standard in recent years.

title: Phase Singularity Enabled Polarization Switchable Analog Spatial Differentiation In An Atomic MoS$_2$ Planar Fabry-P\'erot Cavity
authors: Zhonglin Li (department Of Optoelectronic Science, Harbin Institute Of Technology At Weihai, Weihai 264209, China, Department Of Physics, Harbin Institute Of Technology, Harbin 150001, China), Yingying Wang (department Of Optoelectronic Science, Harbin Institute Of Technology At Weihai, Weihai 264209, China), Jiawei Kang (department Of Optoelectronic Science, Harbin Institute Of Technology At Weihai, Weihai 264209, China), Yangyang Zhang (department Of Optoelectronic Science, Harbin Institute Of Technology At Weihai, Weihai 264209, China), Wenjun Liu (department Of Optoelectronic Science, Harbin Institute Of Technology At Weihai, Weihai 264209, China), Zexiang Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconfigurable analog optical computing requires rapid and efficient switching between core mathematical operations, such as first- and second-order spatial differentiation. Here, we demonstrate a monolayer MoS[MATH] integrated a planar Fabry-P\'erot (F-P) cavity that performs polarization switchable analog spatial differentiation under oblique incidence. By exploiting polarization dependent phase singularities, the device satisfies distinct optical transfer functions for different-order differentiation at the same operating condition. As a result, first-order and second-order derivatives of input images are experimentally realized by simply switching the incident polarization. These results establish the planar cavity as a compact reconfigurable spatial differentiator, whose computational order is controlled solely by light polarization. This approach provides a fast, convenient, and integration friendly strategy for tunable optical computing, and enables polarization switchable edge detection for image processing, with potential applications in real-time object recognition, feature extraction, and optical data compression.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a polarization-switchable analog spatial differentiator using a monolayer MoS2 integrated Fabry-Pérot cavity, enabling first- and second-order edge detection by switching incident polarization.
motivation: Reconfigurable analog optical computing requires rapid switching between mathematical operations; existing devices lack fast, compact, and integration-friendly tunability.
method: A monolayer MoS2 planar Fabry-Pérot cavity is designed to exploit polarization-dependent phase singularities, achieving distinct optical transfer functions for different-order differentiation at the same operating condition.
result: First-order and second-order derivatives of input images are experimentally realized by simply switching the incident polarization, demonstrating polarization-switchable edge detection.
conclusion: The planar cavity provides a compact, reconfigurable spatial differentiator whose computational order is controlled solely by light polarization, offering a fast and integration-friendly strategy for tunable optical computing.

title: A Parametric Theory Of Vector Spaces With Applications To Fuzzy Vector Spaces
authors: Hasan Haddadzadeh Bayaz Daraby
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose a parameterized framework for vector spaces in which each vector is represented by a family of parameter-dependent realizations.
tldr: This paper proposes a parametric framework for vector spaces with parameter-dependent realizations, applied to fuzzy vector spaces.
motivation: To generalize vector spaces by introducing a parameterized representation that can capture fuzziness or uncertainty.
method: The authors define a family of vector spaces parameterized by a parameter, and develop the theory of such parametric vector spaces, including applications to fuzzy vector spaces.
result: A new parametric theory of vector spaces is established, with connections to fuzzy vector spaces.
conclusion: The parametric framework provides a flexible tool for modeling vector spaces with inherent uncertainty, but the paper is purely mathematical and unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Rule-Induced Behavior Of Fuzzy Scalar Objective Functions For Reliable Multi-Criteria Decision Making
authors: Olaf Frommann
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fuzzy-rule-based scalar objective functions provide a flexible way to encode qualitative preferences, reference regions, and interactions between criteria in multi-criteria optimization and decision making. However, the scalar preference landscape induced by such rules can differ substantially from the intended decision semantics. This paper investigates how membership placement, implicit single-criterion baseline rules, and explicit rule consequents affect the behavior of fuzzy scalar objective functions. Two analytically controlled bi-criteria Pareto fronts and an embedded two-dimensional dominated-reference formulation are used to separate front-selection mechanisms from reference improvement behavior. The study shows that apparent reference following can be caused by flat rule-activation plateaus, whereas genuine reference following requires localized minima with low tie ambiguity. In the dominated-reference setting, global memberships with competing consequents recover robust Pareto tradeoffs but do not necessarily improve each reference design. By contrast, a reference-based three-class rule set consistently improves dominated references, recovers the Pareto set, and avoids plateau-driven selection in the present tests. The results provide diagnostic metrics and practical guidance for constructing fuzzy scalarizations whose optimization behavior is consistent with the intended decision semantics.
tldr: This paper studies fuzzy-rule-based scalar objective functions for multi-criteria decision making, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Fuzzy scalarizations are used in multi-criteria optimization, but their behavior may not match intended decision semantics.
method: The author analyzes membership placement, baseline rules, and rule consequents using bi-criteria Pareto fronts and a dominated-reference formulation.
result: Apparent reference following can arise from flat rule-activation plateaus; genuine reference following requires localized minima. A three-class rule set consistently improves dominated references.
conclusion: Diagnostic metrics and guidelines are provided to construct fuzzy scalarizations with consistent optimization behavior.

title: Li--Yorke Chaos Along Any Infinite Sequence: Relative Mixing, Sofic And Rokhlin Entropy
authors: Chunlin Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a countably infinite discrete group and let [MATH] be a nontrivial relatively mixing extension, where [MATH] is a compact metrizable [MATH]-space. We prove that there exists a constant [MATH] such that, for every injective sequence [MATH] in [MATH], there is a Cantor set [MATH] whose distinct points [MATH] satisfy \[ \liminf_{i\to\infty}\rho(s_i x,s_i x')=0, \qquad \limsup_{i\to\infty}\rho(s_i x,s_i x')>\delta. \] The method also yields higher-order scrambled Cantor sets. As a principal application, for a sofic group [MATH], positive topological sofic entropy implies the preceding conclusion, answering a question of Huang, Li, and Ye. The same conclusion also holds for actions of arbitrary countably infinite discrete groups admitting an essentially free invariant measure of positive Rokhlin entropy.
tldr: This paper proves Li-Yorke chaos for relatively mixing extensions of group actions, linking to sofic and Rokhlin entropy.
motivation: To understand chaotic behavior in dynamical systems beyond classical settings, specifically for actions of countably infinite discrete groups.
method: Uses relative mixing extensions and constructs scrambled Cantor sets via combinatorial and ergodic theory techniques.
result: Shows that positive topological sofic entropy implies Li-Yorke chaos along any infinite sequence, answering a question by Huang, Li, and Ye.
conclusion: The results extend known chaos theory to sofic groups and actions with positive Rokhlin entropy, but have no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Pipelined Gradient Coding
authors: Jun Li Xian Su
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In large-scale machine learning, distributed training commonly involves multiple workers evaluating the gradients of the model on different dataset partitions. A common challenge is the presence of straggling workers, which may significantly slow down training. Traditional gradient coding (GC) addresses this by duplicating dataset partitions across workers, allowing for the replacement of missing gradients from stragglers. However, GC requires workers to evaluate gradients on multiple dataset partitions in each step, potentially increasing overall training time. In this paper, we propose to pipeline GC, such that gradient evaluation is segmented across multiple steps and each worker evaluates gradients on just a single dataset partition per step. We develop the pipelined version for fractional repetition (FR) and cyclic repetition (CR), two representative dataset placement schemes in GC, and prove convergence guarantees for both. Through extensive simulations and experiments on cloud infrastructure, our schemes not only significantly reduce training time but also accelerate convergence compared to GC and other baselines.
tldr: This paper proposes pipelined gradient coding to mitigate stragglers in distributed machine learning, reducing training time and accelerating convergence.
motivation: Distributed training suffers from straggling workers that slow down training; traditional gradient coding duplicates data partitions, increasing per-step workload.
method: The authors pipeline gradient evaluation across multiple steps so each worker processes only one partition per step, and develop pipelined versions for fractional repetition and cyclic repetition placement schemes with convergence proofs.
result: Simulations and cloud experiments show that pipelined gradient coding significantly reduces training time and accelerates convergence compared to standard gradient coding and other baselines.
conclusion: Pipelining gradient coding effectively mitigates straggler effects without increasing per-step workload, offering a practical improvement for large-scale distributed learning.

title: Asymptotic Contractivity Of The Bohnenblust--Hille Inequality For Polynomials With Few Interacting Variables
authors: Jorge Nicol\'as Caro Montoya, Daniel N\'u\~nez Alarc\'on, Diana Marcela Serrano Rodr\'iguez
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] denote the optimal Bohnenblust--Hille constant on the class of [MATH]-homogeneous polynomials all of whose monomials involve at most [MATH] different variables. We prove that, for every fixed [MATH], these constants are asymptotically contractive: \[ \lim_{m\to\infty}K_{m,M}=1. \] More precisely, \[ 1\le K_{m,M}\le A_M^{M/m}m^{(M^2-1)/(2m)}, \] where [MATH] depends only on [MATH]. The argument combines bounded projections onto exact support levels, a random colouring of the active variables, the classical multilinear Bohnenblust--Hille inequality and interpolation with Parseval's identity. We also point out that the qualitative conclusion follows from a recent, more general support-sensitive Bohnenblust--Hille inequality, although its direct application gives a slightly larger power of the homogeneous degree.
tldr: This paper proves asymptotic contractivity of the Bohnenblust-Hille constant for polynomials with few interacting variables.
motivation: The Bohnenblust-Hille inequality is a classical result in analysis; understanding its constants for polynomials with limited variable interactions is a technical question in functional analysis.
method: The proof combines bounded projections onto exact support levels, random coloring of active variables, the classical multilinear Bohnenblust-Hille inequality, and interpolation with Parseval's identity.
result: For fixed number of variables M, the constants K_{m,M} tend to 1 as the degree m grows, with explicit bounds provided.
conclusion: The result confirms asymptotic contractivity, which is a purely mathematical finding with no direct application to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Two-Sample Test On Weighted Persistence Intensity Functions In Topological Data Analysis
authors: Yeongung Han, Ilmun Kim, Jisu Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The intensity function, defined as the Lebesgue density of the expected measure of a persistence diagram, is a fundamental summary of the probability distribution of persistence diagrams in topological data analysis (TDA). Although several methods have been proposed for estimating intensity functions, statistical hypothesis testing for intensity functions remains largely unexplored. In particular, little is known about the power properties of hypothesis tests based on persistence diagrams. We propose a kernel-based permutation test and analyze its power against alternatives characterized by differences in persistence intensity functions. We introduce assumptions that control the effect of the possibly unbounded cardinality of persistence diagrams and yield a sharp variance bound for the test statistic. We also show that our probability model is broad enough to include all probability densities on the subset of [MATH] where [MATH]. Using these results, we establish minimax optimality of the proposed test. Along the way, we derive an explicit characterization of the persistence diagram of the ech complex on the circle. Since the optimal bandwidth is not directly accessible in practice, we adopt a bandwidth aggregation framework. Simulations and real-data applications demonstrate validity and high empirical power.
tldr: This paper proposes a kernel-based permutation test for weighted persistence intensity functions in topological data analysis.
motivation: Statistical hypothesis testing for intensity functions of persistence diagrams is largely unexplored, and little is known about power properties of such tests.
method: The authors introduce a kernel-based permutation test, derive a sharp variance bound under assumptions controlling unbounded cardinality, and adopt a bandwidth aggregation framework.
result: The test is shown to be minimax optimal, and simulations and real-data applications demonstrate high empirical power.
conclusion: The proposed test provides a valid and powerful method for two-sample testing on persistence intensity functions.

title: One Residual Set Of Cantor Graphs With Dense Conjugacy Classes
authors: Zhengyu Yin
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we consider the space [MATH] of all closed graphs on the Cantor set [MATH]. Equipping this space with Hausdorff metric and employing combinatorial methods, we see that the residual isomorphism classes in the space of single-valued continuous maps on the Cantor set are no longer a [MATH] set but still dense in [MATH], and we prove that the set consisting of elements with dense conjugacy classes is a dense [MATH] subset of [MATH]. Finally, we prove that the set consisting of elements with zero topological entropy is a dense [MATH] set in [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies residual sets of Cantor graphs with dense conjugacy classes and zero topological entropy, using combinatorial methods and Hausdorff metric.
motivation: The work explores topological properties of closed graphs on the Cantor set, specifically focusing on residual isomorphism classes and conjugacy classes.
method: The author equips the space of closed graphs with the Hausdorff metric and uses combinatorial methods to analyze residual sets and topological entropy.
result: It is shown that the set of elements with dense conjugacy classes is a dense Gδ subset, and the set of elements with zero topological entropy is also a dense Gδ set.
conclusion: The paper provides a characterization of residual sets in the space of Cantor graphs, but the topic is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: High-Order Exponential Integrators With Improved Uniform Accuracy For Charged-Particle In A Perpendicular Strong Magnetic Field
authors: Weibing Deng Zhihao Qi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper considers a class of charged-particle dynamics problems in which the particle is subjected to a magnetic force, with a magnetic flux density inversely proportional to a small parameter [MATH], and a nonlinear electric force. The resulting highly oscillatory behavior poses significant challenges for numerical computation. To enhance the performance of exponential integrators (EIs), this paper employs a technique that linearizes the ordinary differential equation through a dimension-raising approach. Based on this technique, a new family of EIs is developed that achieves arbitrarily high order. For short-time simulations on the interval [MATH], it is rigorously proved that the proposed method--which employs auxiliary polynomials of degree [MATH] and a time step [MATH]--satisfies two distinct error bounds: [MATH] and [MATH]. The latter bound guarantees that the algorithm stays accurate even when the step size is of order [MATH]. Furthermore, when a large step size [MATH] is used to simulate the long-term dynamics over [MATH], the numerical scheme attains a uniform convergence rate of [MATH]. Several numerical experiments confirm these theoretical results.
tldr: This paper develops high-order exponential integrators for charged-particle dynamics in a strong magnetic field, focusing on numerical analysis rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Simulating charged-particle motion in a strong magnetic field is computationally challenging due to high oscillations; existing methods lack uniform accuracy for large step sizes.
method: A dimension-raising technique linearizes the ODE, enabling construction of exponential integrators with arbitrary order; error bounds are proved for both short-time and long-time regimes.
result: The proposed integrators achieve uniform convergence rates of O(h^m) for short-time and O(h^2) for long-time simulations, even with step sizes of order epsilon.
conclusion: The new family of exponential integrators significantly improves accuracy and efficiency for charged-particle dynamics in strong magnetic fields.

title: Dyadic Resolvent Representations Of Self-Adjoint Operators: Propagator Expansions, Spectral Measures, And Zeta Functions
authors: Nicholas Castillo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a self-adjoint operator [MATH] on a Hilbert space, the dyadic resolvent representation of Castillo, Costin and Costin expresses the resolvent [MATH] as a series in the unitary group [MATH] sampled at the dyadic times [MATH]. We develop this representation structurally and through several spectral applications. We first exhibit the underlying operators as a one-parameter scale family obeying a Landen doubling recursion whose telescoping recovers the representation, and record its readings as a series of Zak transforms and as a dyadic filter bank. As a worked instance of the Zak-transform reading we obtain dyadic-Bessel series for the lattice Green functions of [MATH], with closed-form special values: the lemniscatic constant [MATH] in two dimensions and Watson's integral in three. For the Laplacian [MATH] on [MATH] we expand [MATH], for [MATH], as a series of convolutions with the free Schr\"odinger propagator, and derive explicit dyadic representations of the fundamental solutions of the Laplace and Poisson equations in [MATH] and of the one-dimensional heat equation. Finally, we reconstruct spectral data of [MATH] from the dyadic representation: the spectral measures on [MATH], including, through the limiting absorption principle, the absolutely continuous spectral density of [MATH], together with the density of states and the spectral zeta function, the last reducing to the Riemann zeta function for [MATH] on the circle and yielding the functional determinant of [MATH] there. We close by showing that the dyadic samples determine [MATH] uniquely, an exact anti-aliasing of the propagator, so that all of this spectral data is a function of the dyadic samples alone.
tldr: This paper develops a dyadic resolvent representation for self-adjoint operators and applies it to spectral theory, including expansions of propagators and spectral measures.
motivation: To provide a structural development of the dyadic resolvent representation and demonstrate its utility in spectral analysis of differential operators.
method: The representation is derived via a Landen doubling recursion and interpreted through Zak transforms and dyadic filter banks; applications to Laplacians on Euclidean space and the circle are worked out.
result: Explicit dyadic series for lattice Green functions, fundamental solutions of Laplace/Poisson/heat equations, and spectral data (spectral measures, density of states, zeta function) are obtained.
conclusion: The dyadic samples uniquely determine the operator, enabling spectral reconstruction from propagator samples at dyadic times.

title: On The Approximation Of The Unitary Operator Group Associated With A Rotation Matrix And Its Applications To Abstract Hyperbolic Equations
authors: Zurab Vashakidze Jemal Rogava
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The solution of the Cauchy problem for homogeneous abstract hyperbolic equations, together with its derivative, admits a vector representation in terms of a unitary operator group associated with a rotation matrix. A rational approximation of this unitary group is constructed and shown to possess optimal fourth-order convergence. The order of convergence is determined in accordance with the smoothness scale. Based on this rational approximation, a two-layer semi-discrete scheme is constructed for the approximate solution of Cauchy problems for nonhomogeneous abstract hyperbolic equations in both the linear and semi-linear settings. The convergence properties of the scheme are examined in relation to the regularity of the solution.
tldr: This paper presents a rational approximation of a unitary operator group associated with a rotation matrix for solving abstract hyperbolic equations.
motivation: To construct efficient numerical schemes for abstract hyperbolic equations with optimal convergence order.
method: A rational approximation of the unitary operator group is derived, and a two-layer semi-discrete scheme is built for nonhomogeneous linear and semi-linear hyperbolic equations.
result: The approximation achieves optimal fourth-order convergence, with convergence properties depending on solution regularity.
conclusion: The proposed scheme provides an efficient numerical method for abstract hyperbolic equations.

title: Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov Inclusions Of The Mean Field Type
authors: Yurii Averboukh
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The paper studies a dynamical system in the Wasserstein space, where the evolution is governed by a Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov equation with coefficients chosen from a prescribed set that depends at each point on that point and on the current measure. Under the assumption that the multivalued mapping determining the constraints is convex-valued, upper semicontinuous and satisfies certain growth conditions, we prove an existence theorem and establish the compactness of the solution set. Moreover, we study an optimal control problem for such dynamical systems.
tldr: This paper studies mean field type dynamical systems governed by Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov inclusions and optimal control in Wasserstein space.
motivation: The paper aims to establish existence and compactness results for solutions of Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov inclusions with set-valued coefficients, and to study optimal control problems for such systems.
method: The authors assume the multivalued mapping is convex-valued, upper semicontinuous, and satisfies growth conditions, then prove an existence theorem and compactness of the solution set using techniques from differential inclusions and optimal control theory.
result: An existence theorem for solutions of the Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov inclusion is proved, along with compactness of the solution set, and an optimal control problem is analyzed.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for mean field type control problems with set-valued dynamics, but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: PhantomSeal: Proactive Deepfakes Defense With Identity/Context Protection And Forensic Tracing
authors: Liangqin Ren, Zeyan Liu, Ye Wang, Yuxin Chen, Fengjun Li, Bo Luo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deepfakes, especially face-swapping attacks, pose significant challenges to authenticity, security, and ethics across science, engineering, and society. While most existing detection/tracing approaches operate post hoc, proactive defenses that aim to intervene before deepfake generation remain limited in terms of real-world effectiveness. In this paper, we present PhantomSeal, the first proactive defense to simultaneously protect both the identity and the context of users' images from being used in face-swapping attacks, while supporting forensic tracing. We present a novel cloaking technique that embeds a selected identity as a stealthy identifier. This mechanism steers the deepfake generation process toward producing content that resembles the chosen cloak identity, thereby preventing successful face-swapping while enabling effective feature-based forensic analysis. The effectiveness and robustness of PhantomSeal is demonstrated in extensive experiments across different face-swapping architectures and models. For example, it reduces the attack success rate of SimSwap, an advanced deepfake model, to 0.30%, and correctly identifies 97.97% of manipulated content. Codes can be found at [URL].
tldr: This paper presents a proactive defense against deepfake face-swapping attacks by embedding a stealthy identifier to protect identity and context while enabling forensic tracing.
motivation: Existing deepfake defenses are mostly post hoc and limited in real-world effectiveness; proactive methods that intervene before generation are needed.
method: The authors propose a cloaking technique that embeds a selected identity as a stealthy identifier, steering deepfake generation toward the cloak identity and preventing successful face-swapping.
result: Experiments show the method reduces attack success rate of SimSwap to 0.30% and correctly identifies 97.97% of manipulated content.
conclusion: PhantomSeal is the first proactive defense to simultaneously protect identity and context while supporting forensic tracing, demonstrating high effectiveness and robustness.

title: Deepfake News Detection: A Multimodal Framework Integrating LipNet, DeepSpeech And ResNET For Enhanced Audio-Visual Analysis
authors: Ameena Khan, Muhammad Ahsan Aziz, Muhammad Junaid Asif, Naeem Akhter, Rana Fayyaz Ahmad
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deepfake news refers to AI-generated (or AI ma-nipulated) multimedia content intentionally generated to deceive audiences by manipulating the facial expressions, or speech while maintaining the realistic appearance. The rapid progress of generative AI has made the synthesis of highly realistic fake videos and cloned voices widely accessible, posing a serious threat to the authenticity of digital news media. This paper presents a multi-modal framework that discerns the authenticity of video content by jointly exploiting audio and visual cues, thereby addressing the challenge of detecting the deepfake videos. We proposed a framework that involves features extraction from lip movements, audio content and video frames. Lip movements and speech content are encoded using the LipNet and DeepSpeech2 models, while facial features are extracted by leveraging the use of BlazeFace and represented with ResNet18. The extracted feature vectors are concatenated into a holistic video representation and classified with an ensemble of machine learning and deep learning models, including Random Forest (RF), Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Exten-sive experiments performed on the FakeAVCeleb dataset shows that the proposed approach attains an accuracy of 94% using augmented audio features, outperforming a state-of-the-art multi-modal ensemble baseline. The results confirm the robustness and practical potential of the proposed framework for deepfake news detection.
tldr: A multimodal deepfake news detection framework combining lip movement, audio, and visual features.
motivation: Deepfake news poses a threat to digital media authenticity; existing detection methods often rely on single modalities.
method: Extracts features using LipNet, DeepSpeech2, and ResNet18, then classifies with an ensemble of RF, MLP, and LSTM.
result: Achieves 94% accuracy on the FakeAVCeleb dataset, outperforming a state-of-the-art baseline.
conclusion: The proposed multimodal framework is robust and effective for deepfake news detection.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models For Symbolic Security Protocol Analysis
authors: Paolo Modesti, Syed Ahmed, Ioannis Sfyrakis, Derek Enodolomwanyi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security protocol verification relies on formal tools such as ProVerif and OFMC. This study evaluates whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can perform comparable analysis. We test GPT and DeepSeek in chat and reasoning modes over three runs on 130 obfuscated AnB/AnBx protocols covering 388 security goals, scored against ProVerif and OFMC. Chat models reach 69 to 81% recall at precision below 31%. Reasoning models reverse this trade-off, reaching 66.5% precision for GPT and 45.4% for DeepSeek, but detect just over half the attacks. DeepSeek's two modes share one underlying model, so the comparison isolates reasoning itself, which raises precision from 27.2% to 45.4%. The GPT contrast spans a model-version change and is only suggestive. All models perform worst on authentication goals: reasoning models detect well under half of injective and non-injective agreement attacks, whereas chat models over-flag them at low precision. Confidentiality is the exception, with F1 up to 95.7% in reasoning mode. Verdicts are unstable across runs, identical on 89.7% of goals for GPT but 74.0% for DeepSeek. Self-reported confidence is uniformly high yet shows no meaningful correlation with correctness. On this benchmark LLMs do not match formal verification, but may serve, at best, as pre-screening filters.
tldr: Evaluates LLMs for symbolic security protocol analysis, finding they do not match formal verification tools.
motivation: To determine if LLMs can replace or augment formal verification tools like ProVerif and OFMC for security protocol analysis.
method: Tested GPT and DeepSeek in chat and reasoning modes on 130 obfuscated protocols with 388 security goals, scoring against ProVerif and OFMC.
result: Chat models achieve 69-81% recall with low precision; reasoning models improve precision (up to 66.5%) but detect only half the attacks. Performance is unstable across runs.
conclusion: LLMs are not yet reliable for security protocol verification but may serve as pre-screening filters.

title: Operational Identity: A Finite Audit Of Declared And Implemented Rules Of Sameness
authors: Denise M. Case
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A record system declares when two records refer to the same entity, occurrence, scope, or rule. Its disclosed implementation mechanisms induce a corresponding operational identity relation. The declared and implemented relations may diverge systematically without producing a provenance gap or detectable contradiction. A system can apply, consistently and with every record individually correct, a rule of sameness that no artifact declares. This paper formalizes that implemented relation. A declared identity regime partitions a finite record domain into co-reference classes; a disclosed mechanism, through its typed identity-relevant outcomes, induces an operational identity partition of the same domain. The audit compares these partitions in the refinement lattice. A mechanism is faithful when the declared partition refines the operational partition, so no declared class is split. A divergence witness is a pair the declaration merges and the mechanism separates; such witnesses are decidable by pair enumeration. When an imported sibling basis also splits a declared class, local comparison with its partition yields sibling-aligned, sub-sibling, super-sibling, or sibling-incomparable divergence. This result reports only the relationship; it does not identify the basis carried by the mechanism. Global equality of the operational and sibling partitions is defined separately as regime substitution and does not follow from sibling alignment. A version field incremented on every textual edit inhabits the sub-sibling case by splitting declared classes more finely than either imported basis. The audit is three-valued and relative to the disclosed artifacts, evaluated surfaces, and identified uses; each boundary has a finite refuting witness. A passing verdict is non-monotone because extending the transformation history can merge declared classes and create a witness among records already examined.
tldr: The paper formalizes a finite audit of declared versus implemented identity relations in record systems, using partition refinement and divergence witnesses.
motivation: To detect systematic divergences between declared and implemented rules of sameness in record systems without requiring a provenance gap.
method: The audit compares declared and operational partitions in the refinement lattice, identifies divergence witnesses via pair enumeration, and evaluates sibling-aligned divergence.
result: A three-valued audit relative to disclosed artifacts, with finite refuting witnesses; passing verdict is non-monotone under extended transformation history.
conclusion: The audit provides a formal method to verify faithfulness of identity mechanisms, but does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Classical Acceptance Is Not Hybrid Authentication: Measuring X.509 Verifier Semantics In Post-Quantum Migration
authors: Taesung Kim, Boheung Chung, Keonwoo Kim, Yousung Kang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A relying party validating a hybrid X.509 certificate --- carrying both a classical and a post-quantum credential --- must distinguish whether its accepting judgment rests on the post-quantum evidence or only on the classical path. To preserve compatibility, the separable designs place that evidence where classical path validation may ignore it. A verifier can then validate the classical path and accept while the post-quantum evidence never bears on the decision --- a valid classical result silently promoted to a hybrid conclusion it did not establish. We measure this across eight path-validation stacks (seven independent codebases), in nine validation modes, over six certificate schemes. Under a hybrid-required policy, nearly every stack parsing a separable hybrid certificate accepts on the classical path without making the post-quantum evidence outcome-bearing; one enforcing mode instead fractures interoperability over a signature-input encoding not yet interoperably profiled; and stacks that verify post-quantum signatures still do not enforce the binding by default: the gap is structural, not explained by missing primitive capability alone. Under lifecycle desynchronization the downgrade is realized: when a bound post-quantum credential is revoked while the classical certificate stays valid, the default path still accepts, because the bound credential lies outside the decision's scope. Binding success is not authentication success. We contribute a specification-derived verifier model and an executable, policy-parametric reference contract --- what a verifier must recognize, verify, make outcome-bearing, and check before reporting a validation as hybrid --- with a diagnosis of why standards do not require it.
tldr: This paper analyzes the security of hybrid X.509 certificates in post-quantum migration, revealing that classical acceptance can be mistaken for hybrid authentication.
motivation: Hybrid certificates combining classical and post-quantum credentials may be accepted based solely on the classical path, undermining post-quantum security guarantees.
method: The authors measure the behavior of eight path-validation stacks across nine validation modes and six certificate schemes, and develop a verifier model to diagnose the gap.
result: Nearly all stacks accept on the classical path without making post-quantum evidence outcome-bearing; revocation of the post-quantum credential does not prevent acceptance.
conclusion: Current standards do not require verifiers to ensure post-quantum evidence is outcome-bearing, leading to a structural downgrade vulnerability.

title: Talking Ink: A Flow-Based Multi-Molecule Molecular Communication Testbed For Effective Channel Modeling And Detector Benchmarking
authors: Alexander Wietfeld, Krupakar Duvva, Jiachen Xiao, Wolfgang Kellerer
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20802v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Practical molecular communication (MC) testbeds are essential for translating theoretical concepts toward future applications while retaining physical realism, accessibility, and experimental repeatability. We present a flowbased MC experimental system for real-time multi-molecule (MUMO) transmission using cyan, magenta, and yellow inks as distinguishable molecule-like signaling carriers. Three micropumps and a multi-needle injection system release the inks into a background-flow channel, and a non-invasive spectral sensor estimates received color traces at variable transmitter-receiver distances. The platform supports measurements of isolated-pulse responses across distances. We interpret these measurements as effective end-to-end channel impulse responses (CIRs) shaped by finite release, flow propagation, and receiver readout, and compare two compact model families. Both reproduce much of the dominant arrival timing and pulse shape, while late-tail mismatch remains the main limitation. We connect this channel characterization to communication performance through continuous MUMO on-off keying (OOK) payload measurements. The resulting retrospective benchmark with full-data parameter optimization includes traceonly and CIR-assisted methods. We introduce modified energydifference detection (MEDD), an adaptive extension of standard energy-difference detection (EDD). MEDD outperforms all other trace-only detectors with 34/4500 = 0.76% bit error rate (BER) and closely approaches the best overall minimum mean-square error (MMSE) result of 32/4500 = 0.71%. After targeted parameter tuning, the detector benchmark produces zero errors over the evaluated payloads at 6 bit/s over 8 cm and at 3 bit/s over 24 cm. Overall, the results establish the platform as a reusable experimental setup for effective channel modeling, practical detector benchmarking, and future multi-molecule networking experiments.
tldr: A flow-based molecular communication testbed using colored inks for channel modeling and detector benchmarking.
motivation: To provide a practical, repeatable experimental platform for molecular communication research, bridging theory and real-world implementation.
method: Three micropumps inject cyan, magenta, and yellow inks into a flow channel; a spectral sensor measures color traces; channel impulse responses are modeled and detectors (including a novel MEDD) are benchmarked.
result: The MEDD detector achieves 0.76% BER, approaching the best MMSE result of 0.71%; zero-error transmission is achieved at 6 bit/s over 8 cm and 3 bit/s over 24 cm after tuning.
conclusion: The platform is effective for channel modeling and detector benchmarking, supporting future multi-molecule networking experiments.

title: Which Model Is Actually Serving You? Iris: Budgeted Black-Box Auditing Of Model Substitution And Routing Dilution In Llm Gateways
authors: Yuewei Zhang, Zhi-Hai Zhang, Hanzhang Qin
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Commercial LLM gateways mediate access to hosted models, but the served backend may not match the advertised one: it may substitute a cheaper model on every request or route only a fraction [MATH] of requests to it. Prior black-box auditors often need a privileged signal (log-probabilities, token ranks, or reference samples) or a target-specific probe, fix the query budget in advance, and return a yes/no verdict. We present [MATH], an audit that needs only the returned text: it asks endpoints to generate random numbers or strings, fingerprints the backend, and is the first to combine, in one text-only audit, detection of whole-stream substitution and fractional dilution, attribution of the served backend, routing-fraction ([MATH]) estimation, and a query budget it sizes itself. A cheap pilot fits the exponential query-error decay and freezes that budget before any suspect query is issued. On an intra-family Qwen3 ladder [MATH] verifies the backend at [MATH] AUROC and sharpens attribution as queries accumulate; across a commercial OpenRouter library it catches [MATH] dilution on margin-qualified pairs at [MATH] mean power ([MATH] false-positive rate) and recovers [MATH] to within [MATH] for enrolled diluents; and a live cross-provider audit flags [MATH] of [MATH] same-model provider pairs by genuine quantization and kernel deviations, corroborated on third-party MET traces. Against comparable black-box auditors, [MATH] matches or beats detection on shared tasks, and adaptive allocation lifts the matched-budget target-hit rate from [MATH]% to [MATH]%. Further experiments cover adversarial gateways, knob identifiability, unseen diluents, and false-positive control.
tldr: This paper presents a black-box auditing method for detecting model substitution and routing dilution in commercial LLM gateways using only returned text.
motivation: Commercial LLM gateways may serve cheaper or different models than advertised, and existing auditors require privileged signals or fixed budgets.
method: The method, Iris, fingerprints the backend by asking endpoints to generate random numbers or strings, uses a pilot to adaptively size the query budget, and estimates routing fractions.
result: Iris achieves high AUROC for backend verification, detects dilution with high power, and recovers routing fractions accurately across various settings.
conclusion: Iris provides an effective text-only audit for LLM gateways, matching or surpassing comparable auditors while being budget-efficient.

title: Representative Sets In Propositional Abduction
authors: Johannes Schmidt (j\"onk\"oping University), Mohamed Maizia (j\"onk\"oping University, Link\"oping University), Victor Lagerkvist (link\"oping University), Johannes K. Fichte
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The propositional abduction problem is a well-known form of non-monotonic reasoning where we are asked to find an explanation of a given manifestation. Recently, there has been an influx of results asking more refined questions about the solution space rather than only individual solutions. For example, we might be interested in finding two solutions that are sufficiently far from each other (diverse solutions) in the solution space. In this paper we consider a related representation question where we ask if a given set of explanations S can represent any other explanation (that is, whether their symmetric difference is smaller than a given k). We first study this problem from a classical complexity perspective and obtain a complete classification. While only a handful of cases are tractable, the increase in complexity compared to classical abduction is often smaller than expected. We then study the parameterized complexity for several parameters and obtain new tractable and hard cases. Interestingly, a full parameterized complexity classification would require resolving the parameterized complexity of the covering radius problem from coding theory. To the best of our knowledge, no useful relationship between coding theory and non-monotonic reasoning has previously been established, but such connections seemingly become important when asking more complex questions about solution spaces.
tldr: This paper studies the complexity of finding representative sets of explanations in propositional abduction, establishing connections to coding theory.
motivation: To understand whether a given set of explanations can represent all other explanations within a certain symmetric difference, which is a refined question about solution spaces in non-monotonic reasoning.
method: Classical and parameterized complexity analysis, including reductions from the covering radius problem in coding theory.
result: Complete classical complexity classification showing only a few tractable cases; parameterized complexity classification partially resolved, with full resolution requiring progress on the covering radius problem.
conclusion: The problem is generally hard, but the increase in complexity over classical abduction is smaller than expected, and novel connections to coding theory are established.

title: Case Study: Solving P-99 With Lptp And An Llm
authors: Fred Mesnard, Thierry Marianne, \'etienne Payet, Wim Vanhoof
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ninety-Nine Prolog Problems (P-99) is a famous set of Prolog exercises. We solved the first thirty three just by prompting an LLM (Large Language Model). We used Claude from Anthropic. By solved we mean: generate the Prolog code and a test file, run the tests and check whether they pass, then formally prove types, groundness, termination, uniqueness, existence and also sometimes functional correctness with LPTP (Logic Program Theorem Prover). Hence our approach is an experiment in vibe-coding/vericoding of P-99. It is a vibe-coding experiment because we started from informal specifications written in English and let Claude generate the Prolog code. It also fits within vericoding because the LLM proved reliability guarantees on the generated Prolog code. Claude wrote 58 logic procedures, 508 tests, 257 lemmas for a total of 11800 proof lines. We manually checked each file generated by the LLM. We checked the Prolog code, ran the tests, examined the logical statements generated by Claude and proof-checked Claude's proofs with LPTP. This paper describes this experiment and provides the main details so that it can be reproduced by the interested reader.
tldr: This paper uses an LLM to solve Prolog programming exercises and formally verifies the generated code with a theorem prover.
motivation: To explore the feasibility of combining large language models with formal verification for reliable code generation.
method: The authors prompted Claude to generate Prolog code and tests for P-99 problems, then used LPTP to prove properties like type correctness, termination, and functional correctness.
result: Claude generated 58 logic procedures, 508 tests, and 257 lemmas totaling 11800 proof lines; all generated code and proofs were manually checked.
conclusion: The approach demonstrates that LLMs can assist in generating formally verified Prolog code, but the work is primarily about software engineering and formal methods, not quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Scaling Up Formal Representation Of Clinical Trial Protocols In Ensemble Logic Using LLMs: A Preliminary Study
authors: Yan Huang, Xubing Hao, Xiaojin Li, Rashmie Abeysinghe, Xiaoqian Jiang, Licong Cui, Guo-Qiang Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The reliance on unstructured free text for documenting clinical trial protocols creates a significant barrier to automated reasoning, cohort discovery, and trial simulation. The lack of formal structure obscures critical temporal phenotypes, such as dynamic eligibility criteria and event timing constraints. Although Temporal Ensemble Logic (TEL) offers an expressive framework for modeling these elements, manual encoding remains a prohibitive bottleneck. We introduce the CT-TEL workflow: a scalable pipeline leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to translate narrative clinical protocols into TEL formulas. We applied CT-TEL to generate logical models for 23 real-world trials from ClinicalTrials.gov. We evaluated translation fidelity via a back-translation approach, using LLMs to convert TEL formulas back into natural language and measuring semantic similarity against source texts. The resulting semantic retention suggests that LLMs may offer a pathway for mapping informal protocols to computable logic, providing preliminary evidence toward scalable clinical trial emulation within the emerging "Symbolic Biomedicine" paradigm championed by the corresponding author.
tldr: This paper uses LLMs to translate clinical trial protocols into Temporal Ensemble Logic formulas, aiming to enable automated reasoning and cohort discovery.
motivation: Clinical trial protocols are documented in unstructured free text, hindering automated analysis. Manual encoding into formal logic is a bottleneck.
method: The CT-TEL workflow leverages LLMs to convert narrative protocols into TEL formulas, evaluated via back-translation and semantic similarity.
result: Applied to 23 real-world trials, the approach shows promising semantic retention, suggesting LLMs can map informal protocols to computable logic.
conclusion: LLMs offer a pathway for scalable clinical trial emulation within the 'Symbolic Biomedicine' paradigm.

title: Toward Cryptographically Verifiable Authorization For Autonomous Ai Agents: A Security Hypothesis, Preliminary Formal Model, And Proof-of-concept Implementation
authors: D. Fern\'andez-Fern\'andez M. Llamb\'i-Morillas
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly execute actions, invoke tools, and operate on protected resources with limited human oversight. Existing authentication and authorization mechanisms establish identity and delegate authority, but do not inherently provide cryptographic evidence that a concrete request issued by a specific agent satisfies the applicable policy in a specific execution context. This paper hypothesizes that agent authorization can be formalized as a cryptographically verifiable relation, denoted [MATH], that jointly binds an agent principal, a concrete authorization request, an execution context, and the satisfaction of an applicable policy, while selectively preserving the confidentiality of private authorization attributes. We introduce a preliminary formal abstraction for Cryptographically Verifiable Agent Authorization (CVA), define a compact set of candidate security properties including authorization soundness, principal binding, request binding, policy binding, and replay resistance, and provide an executable zero-knowledge proof of concept that instantiates selected elements of the model over a Groth16 zk-SNARK construction. We further identify and formalize the structural separation among identity binding, authorization-request binding, and runtime execution binding as a central open problem in the design of secure agentic systems (a distinction {not explicitly addressed by} current agentic security frameworks) and present a falsifiable research agenda for its resolution.
tldr: This paper proposes a cryptographic framework for verifiable authorization of autonomous AI agents using zero-knowledge proofs.
motivation: Current authorization mechanisms for AI agents lack cryptographic evidence that a request satisfies policy in a specific context.
method: The authors formalize a cryptographically verifiable authorization (CVA) model and implement a proof-of-concept using Groth16 zk-SNARKs.
result: They define security properties (authorization soundness, principal binding, etc.) and demonstrate a zero-knowledge proof-of-concept.
conclusion: The work identifies open problems in binding identity, request, and execution context, and proposes a research agenda.

title: Ensemble Logic For Symbolic Representation Of Sleep Medicine Guidelines
authors: Jiahao Fan, Xiaojin Li, Yan Huang, Xubing Hao, Licong Cui, Guo-Qiang Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) Manual is the clinical standard for polysomnography (PSG) scoring, but its narrative rules can admit multiple reasonable interpretations, contributing to inter-scorer variability and implementation differences across studies and software systems. We present a formal framework for translating sleep-scoring rules into Rational Ensemble Logic (QEL), a dense-time (i.e., a continuous, rational-valued timeline rather than discrete steps) formalism that combines first-order quantification with metric temporal operators. Using an extraction-and-compilation procedure, we identified 18 unique atomic propositions and derived 12 final specifications corresponding to clinically scoreable AASM events. Back-translation of QEL specifications into clinician-facing language retained high semantic fidelity to the original scoring narratives (embedding cosine similarity: 79.3, 95% CI: 79.0--79.7) despite low lexical overlap (ROUGE-L: 18.3, 95 CI: 17.6--18.9). Formalization also clarifies latent ambiguities, including implicit physiological latencies and overlapping exclusions. This framework yields executable, rigorous rule specifications for computational phenotyping, more consistent implementation across datasets, and standardized open-source PSG analysis. This work is a part of the "Symbolic Biomedicine" program championed by the corresponding author.
tldr: This paper formalizes sleep medicine scoring guidelines using a dense-time temporal logic, but is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine Manual's narrative rules lead to inter-scorer variability; a formal framework is needed for consistent implementation.
method: The authors translate sleep-scoring rules into Rational Ensemble Logic (QEL), a dense-time formalism combining first-order quantification with metric temporal operators, and back-translate to clinician-facing language.
result: They identified 18 atomic propositions and derived 12 specifications; back-translation achieved high semantic fidelity (cosine similarity 79.3) despite low lexical overlap (ROUGE-L 18.3).
conclusion: The framework yields executable, rigorous rule specifications for computational phenotyping and standardized PSG analysis.

title: TopoGuard: Graph Theory Based Defenses Against Split-Knowledge Attacks On Rag
authors: Zuobin Xiong Chahana Dahal
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20437v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Production Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems rely on aggregating multiple external documents to answer complex queries. However, the retrieved documents introduce a new threat surface that can be exploited to launch split-knowledge attacks. In this attack, the adversary injects documents that are individually benign but create false associations when combined and fed to language models. This paper shows that the new attack is structurally invisible to existing per-document filters, like LlamaGuard. To address this issue in RAG, this work introduces TopoGuard, a family of graph theory-based methods specifically targeting the split-knowledge attacks by building a semantic similarity graph from retrieved documents and detecting contexts with malicious topology. Grounded on the theoretical analysis, the TopoGuard family has been proven to be effective and robust even with noisy inputs. Extensive experiments are conducted on two retrieval datasets and compared with multiple baseline methods. Specifically, the TopoGuard-[MATH]+Entity catches 21[MATH] more attacks than LlamaGuard-2-8B at 1\% FPR (32.6\% vs 1.5\% recall) on the HotpotQA dataset. Compared with production RAG detection systems using large language models, the proposed TopoGuard variants run efficiently at sub-millisecond latency and stay robust under adaptive adversaries and benign cross-domain queries.
tldr: This paper proposes graph theory-based defenses against split-knowledge attacks on Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems.
motivation: RAG systems are vulnerable to split-knowledge attacks where individually benign documents create false associations when combined, and existing per-document filters fail to detect such attacks.
method: The authors introduce TopoGuard, a family of methods that build a semantic similarity graph from retrieved documents and detect malicious contexts using graph theory.
result: TopoGuard variants achieve significantly higher recall (32.6% vs 1.5%) at 1% FPR compared to LlamaGuard-2-8B on HotpotQA, with sub-millisecond latency.
conclusion: TopoGuard provides effective and robust defense against split-knowledge attacks in RAG systems, outperforming existing methods.

authors: Flavio Del Santo

abstract: Nature Reviews Physics, Published online: 20 July 2026;

result: Schrödinger's views on determinism evolved and were not simply reactionary; he engaged with indeterminism in a radical way.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, covering collective motion in biological and robotic systems.
motivation: To understand how self-alignment of active units with their velocity leads to novel collective behaviors.
method: Unified mathematical framework and review of existing models of self-alignment in active systems.
result: Self-alignment enables orbiting, synchronized motion, and emergent collective phenomena in dense assemblies.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a key mechanism for motion in active matter with applications in biology and robotics.

abstract:
